Selling a house in Jacksonville FAQ

How much is a house worth in Jacksonville?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Jacksonville at $266,100.

How can a Jacksonville homeowner sell fast?

List with an agent, accept a cash offer, or hand the house over untouched to an as-is purchaser who absorbs the repair bill. In each case the deed is signed before two witnesses and recorded with the Duval County clerk. How fast it goes depends on the buyer's financing, the state of title and any lien that needs a payoff letter.

Jacksonville is huge and varied, so the best route changes by property. A tidy house in a popular area can do well in a standard listing. A house needing a roof, rewiring or storm repair, or one tied up by tenants or an estate, often suits a cash or as-is buyer because no lender inspection stands in the way.

  • Listing: biggest buyer pool, longest timeline, lender appraisal and repair requests.
  • Cash or as-is: fewer conditions, you price the condition in.
  • Family transfer: still a conveyance for value, and the homestead rules below still apply.

What sets Jacksonville apart from other Florida cities?

Jacksonville and Duval County merged governments in 1968, and the city calls itself the largest city by area in the continental United States. QuickFacts shows 747.29 land square miles, with 1,017,689 people estimated for July 2025, 7.2 percent above the 2020 base figure. The city's own page cites about 1,007,189 residents, a strong-mayor system and a 19-member council with five at-large and 14 district seats.

One municipal government therefore covers beach communities, a riverfront downtown, suburban subdivisions and rural edges. Permit, utility and code questions go to the same city, yet conditions differ block by block, so a seller should not assume a neighbor's experience applies across town.

The housing picture is more modest than South Florida's. Across 2020 to 2024, the typical owner-occupied house was valued at $293,700, owner-occupants held 57.6 percent of homes, while the middle rent was $1,465. The average commute is 24.1 minutes, and 77,012 residents are veterans, which is one reason the appraiser's exemption list for service members and first responders is long.

The city's regional page adds that Jacksonville and its neighbors work together on growth, transportation and water management, which is worth remembering when you weigh a home's distance from the river and major roads.

What drives Jacksonville's economy and buyer demand?

In its own words the city is the economic driver of a seven-county Northeast Florida region of about 1.7 million people, with port, air cargo, rail and trucking links. It cites a mild climate and a reasonable cost of living as reasons employers relocate here.

Census business totals for 2022 show the scale: roughly $28.6 billion at retail, $12.1 billion in medical and social-service work, and $9.7 billion in transportation and warehousing.

  • Region: the St. Johns River, St. Augustine and Fernandina Beach sit within the same regional area, per the city's overview.
  • Households: 394,370, averaging 2.42 people.
  • Schooling: 91.1 percent of adults finished high school and about a third (33.2 percent) earned a four-year degree or more.

How does Duval's homestead exemption play into a sale?

Your exemption ends with the sale and the buyer files their own. The Duval County Property Appraiser describes a $25,000 exemption, plus up to $25,000 more on value above $50,000 that skips school taxes.

The office states that when a home sells, assessed value goes up to market value for the next tax roll, and the Save Our Homes ceiling of 3 percent or less on yearly increases begins again for the new owner. A buyer who held a Florida homestead in any of the three prior roll years can file for portability, a separate application. The timely date for both is March 1, and late filing runs to early September.

Duval renews exemptions automatically each January 1 when nothing has changed and mails a renewal card as a receipt. The office also has a brochure on how short-term renting can affect exemptions, which landlords should read before listing a house they once lived in. For forms, call 904-255-5900 or email pacustserv@coj.net; the office is at 231 E. Forsyth Street, Suite 260.

Which other Jacksonville exemptions might a buyer or seller mention?

The Duval appraiser's exemption page lists many categories beyond the basic homestead, and a buyer's ability to claim them can shape an offer. Ask the office whether a benefit survives or must be refiled after your sale.

  • Veterans and service members: armed forces deployment, disabled veteran, and service-connected total and permanent disability exemptions.
  • First responders: a total and permanent disability exemption for them and their surviving spouses, and a homestead exemption for surviving spouses of military veterans or first responders.
  • Seniors: a senior citizen exemption with its own application and the Duval 501 form.
  • Other: blindness, widow or widower, disability, a granny-flat assessment reduction for parents' or grandparents' quarters, conservation land, and institutional or non-profit exemptions.
  • Historic preservation: available through the City of Jacksonville.

The page asks people to call or email for several forms, because the website was being updated, so verify that you hold the current version.

What transfer costs and tax dates apply in Jacksonville?

Duval follows the standard state deed rate, set at 70 cents for each $100 paid, and guidance says all signers share liability. A mortgage on the property counts as consideration whether or not the buyer assumes it.

Payment goes to the clerk at the recording counter. Recording fees under section 28.24 begin at $5.00 for a first page and rise with extra pages, names and technology charges.

On the property tax side, value is set January 1, bills come in November, discounts shrink month by month into February, and unpaid bills turn delinquent April 1. The title agent prorates the year at closing. Ask the Duval tax collector for your balance instead of estimating.

Which Jacksonville figures should I keep at hand?

ItemDetailSource
Exemption filingMarch 1; late filing to early SeptemberJacksonville Property Appraiser
Deed tax70 cents for every $100 of the priceSection 201.02
Clerk charge, page one$5.00Section 28.24
Unpaid taxDelinquent April 1State revenue department
Appraiser forms line904-255-5900Jacksonville Property Appraiser

What if the Jacksonville house is in foreclosure, an estate or rented?

  • Foreclosure: after final judgment the clerk sets a public sale 20 to 35 days out unless the lender consents to a longer gap. Homestead owners are told to check with the clerk within 10 days after sale about leftover funds.
  • Estate: summary administration fits a modest estate, meaning $150,000 or under outside exempt assets, or a death over two years ago.
  • Tenants: month-by-month occupants need 30 days' notice. A tenant who raises any defense besides payment must deposit accrued rent with the court within five days of service.

What should I prepare before a Jacksonville buyer visits?

  • Recorded deed, survey if you have one, and the latest tax bill.
  • Payoff letters, and association paperwork for condos and HOAs.
  • Receipts and permits for the roof, systems and any storm repairs.
  • Lease copies and rent ledgers if the house is occupied.
  • For an inherited home, the court order authorizing the sale.

Jacksonville is a single consolidated jurisdiction, so the city is the place to ask about open permits on a property before you list.

More questions about Jacksonville, FL

Does Jacksonville charge a different deed tax?

No. Duval County uses the 70 cents per $100 rate. The revenue department lists only Miami-Dade as different.

When is the Duval homestead deadline?

March 1 each year. The appraiser's page says late filing is allowed through early September, tied to the 25th day after proposed-tax notices are mailed in mid-August.

Does a buyer inherit my homestead benefit?

No. The sale resets assessed value to market value for the next roll, and the buyer applies for their own exemption.

Can I sell with a tenant living there?

Yes. Give the buyer the lease. Tenancies by the month end on 30 days' notice, and an unpaid-rent case starts with a three-day written notice.

Who handles exemption forms?

The Duval County Property Appraiser. Its exemptions page lists 904-255-5900 and pacustserv@coj.net for form requests.

Miami housing at a glance

Miami is in Miami-Dade County.

  • Estimated population, July 1, 2025: 489,812 (Census Bureau).
  • Owner-occupied homes: 58,481. Renter-occupied homes: 131,801, so about 31% of occupied homes are owner-occupied.

Selling a house in Miami FAQ

How much is a house worth in Miami?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Miami at $475,200.

Which selling routes does a Miami homeowner have?

Three routes exist: hire an agent, handle it yourself, or accept cash from an investor who buys without repairs. Each one gives up something, either price, speed or effort, and the best fit hinges on your loan balance, the state of the house and your deadline.

Within Miami's 36.00 square miles of land live an estimated 489,812 people as of July 2025, a rise of 10.8 percent over the 2020 estimates base. The 2020 census density was 12,285.8 per square mile. Housing types vary block to block, so a neighbor's sale is a weak guide to your own price.

  • Agent: the most exposure, plus showings, repair requests and a longer wait.
  • Do it yourself: you price, advertise, negotiate and handle the paperwork.
  • Investor cash: few showings and a quicker close, normally below what a fixed-up listing earns.
  • Keep and rent: only if the zoning and city rules in the next sections allow your plan.

How common is home ownership in Miami?

Renters dominate here. Owners occupy just 30.8 percent of the 194,821 households counted from 2020 through 2024, with 2.32 people in a typical household.

The same Census page records 57.7 percent of residents as foreign-born and 77.2 percent of those five and older using another language at home. Plan for bilingual showings and for a contract the signers fully understand.

Table 1. Miami housing snapshot, Census Bureau, 2020 to 2024

A midpoint hides a wide spread, and a waterfront condo sits far from an inland single-family house. Get a written offer or an appraisal for your own address.

Could I rent my Miami house short term rather than sell?

Seldom. The city holds that houses and duplexes in the T3 and T4-R transect zones are generally ineligible for short-term rental or lodging use, a position it ties to City of Miami v. Airbnb.

Apartment and condo conversions face a longer list: a Certificate of Occupancy, a state lodging license from the Department of Business and Professional Regulation, a Certificate of Use, a Business Tax Receipt and any county approvals. The Certificate of Use then renews every year, and the city may audit or inspect without notice.

Once more than 25 percent of a building's units are used as short-term rentals, the city treats the building as transient, which triggers a change of occupancy classification and extra building code work. Confirm zoning with the city's zoning department before counting on rental income.

What does a Miami closing cost in taxes and fees?

Miami-Dade stands apart on deed stamps. The state revenue department lists a 60 cent rate per hundred dollars plus a 45 cent surtax, and no surtax when the document moves only a single-family dwelling; the other counties use 70 cents.

A mortgage on the property counts toward the price, so paying it off does not shrink the base. Everyone who signs is liable, which makes the payment clause in the contract worth reading closely.

  • Clerk recording, set by section 28.24 of the Florida Statutes.
  • Payoffs for mortgages, judgments and unpaid taxes.
  • A settlement statement from the title company, which you should see before signing.

How do Miami-Dade taxes work when a Miami house sells?

Property tax runs through two county offices, with the appraiser assessing and the tax collector billing. The appraiser says it neither mails bills nor sets or collects taxes, so call the collector about what you owe.

Its public notice says the appraiser certified the 2026 tax roll on October 16, 2026, and that the June 1 estimate of countywide taxable value was $540.7 billion, up 5.5 percent from 2025. To contest a value, a petition must reach the clerk inside a 25-day window that starts with the proposed tax notice, and it is heard by the value adjustment board.

After a homestead sells, the next owner is assessed at full value starting the next January 1. If you are buying again in Florida, ask the appraiser about portability, which is requested with the new homestead filing, due March 1.

How do I handle liens, repairs or code problems in Miami?

A cash sale can still close, but each item has to be cleared or priced. A title search turns up mortgages, judgments and unpaid taxes, and a bill unpaid after April 1 becomes delinquent with certificates sold by June 1.

Open permits and unpermitted work often surface in older buildings. Ask the city's building department what is open on your parcel, and ask the buyer whether the offer takes the work as is.

  • Inherited house: the estate may need a court order naming who can convey title.
  • Past-due mortgage: get the payoff and case status from the lender in writing.
  • Tenant in place: Florida sets a 3-day written demand for unpaid rent, not counting weekends or court holidays, and a 30-day notice to end a monthly tenancy.

What happens once the Miami deed is signed?

At closing the clerk of court records the deed and takes the stamp tax while the title company clears liens. The state names warranty, special warranty, quit claim and trustee's deeds among taxable deeds, so switching the form does not dodge the tax.

The appraiser's site also promotes a no-cost clerk alert that alerts you within a day when a document such as a deed is recorded against your property. Enroll before and after a sale to see what was filed.

Tell the appraiser's office when a homestead property sells, and keep the settlement statement with your tax records.

What help does the Miami-Dade appraiser offer owners?

The appraiser's office runs two public branches, one downtown and one in Cutler Bay, and it schedules appointments online. It also holds neighborhood outreach events where staff review values, exemptions and portability one on one.

Widow and widower exemptions, and disability exemptions for veterans or their surviving spouses, can now be filed online, with document uploads. Agricultural classification applications are online too.

If you suspect homestead exemption fraud on a neighboring property, the appraiser's compliance department takes reports. For a sale, the most useful step is to look up your parcel's exemptions and assessed value online, and bring that printout to any pricing conversation.

How do I size up a Miami cash offer?

Set it against the proceeds of a listing once fees, fix-ups and months of upkeep are subtracted. In the contract, find who pays the deed stamp, the title policy and recording, and what becomes of the deposit.

Ask for the settlement date and the closing agent in writing. Hold off signing the deed until the contract is final, and pay no fee merely to receive an offer. If you cannot decide, request a second offer from a different buyer and compare the terms line by line.

More questions about Miami, FL

Is Miami's deed tax higher than elsewhere in Florida?

Miami-Dade uses 60 cents plus a 45 cent surtax per hundred dollars, and a deed for only a single-family home owes no surtax. Other counties use 70 cents.

Can a Miami single-family house be a short-term rental?

Generally no. The city says single-family and duplex structures in T3 and T4-R transect zones are generally ineligible. Ask the zoning department about your parcel.

Who sends my Miami property tax bill?

The Miami-Dade tax collector does. The property appraiser values the property and states plainly that it mails no bills.

May heirs sell a Miami house they inherited?

Yes, after someone has court authority to sign. Summary administration covers non-exempt estates up to $150,000 or a death that occurred over two years ago.

Is my reduced assessment passed to the next owner?

No. The buyer starts at full assessed value after the next January 1, although you could move your saved amount to your next Florida homestead.

Selling a house in Tampa FAQ

How much is a house worth in Tampa?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Tampa at $375,300.

Which route sells a Tampa house fastest?

A cash sale is usually fastest, with no appraisal and no buyer loan to fall through. A listing reaches more buyers but moves slower.

Tampa's estimate is 413,554 residents, a 7.3% climb since April 2020, on 114.02 square miles of land. Owned homes have a 2020 to 2024 median value of $420,400.

What is Tampa's history, and how does it show up in houses?

Fort Brooke was established in 1824 to guard the harbor, and the city grew after Henry B. Plant's 1884 railroad extension and the phosphate boom of the late 1880s. The city's history page says the port is now the seventh largest in the nation. Vicente Martinez Ybor opened a cigar factory in 1886, and Ybor City covers about 2 square miles today.

A building boom from 1923 to 1926 produced many subdivisions, including Davis Island, a man-made island. Houses from that era carry old wiring, plumbing and roofs, which is why cash buyers who accept work are common on Tampa listings.

What are Tampa's older neighborhoods like for sellers?

The city describes Historic Hyde Park as Tampa's oldest existing neighborhood, just west of downtown across the Hillsborough River, with homes from the 1920s and 1930s in a distinct Florida architectural style, shaded streets and quick access to Bayshore Boulevard. Ybor City, about 2 square miles, is Tampa's National Historic Landmark District.

Historic districts can carry design review for exterior changes, so a seller or buyer in one should ask the city's historic preservation office before planning work. Houses of that age also tend to have older wiring and plumbing, which cash buyers factor into an offer.

Does MacDill Air Force Base affect Tampa home sales?

It can. The city's history page notes that U.S. Central Command and U.S. Special Operations Command are headquartered at MacDill Air Force Base, so military moves and orders create steady turnover. Service members who must relocate on short notice often need a quick sale and a clean closing date.

If you are on orders, tell the buyer your latest move date at the start, and ask your closing agent how soon a signed deed can be recorded. A buyer who knows your hard stop can plan around it, and a power of attorney arranged ahead of time lets a trusted person sign if you have already left.

What are the steps from offer to closing in Tampa?

The path is short once a buyer is chosen.

  1. Sign the purchase agreement and open title work with a closing agent.
  2. The agent searches records for liens, back taxes and ownership gaps.
  3. You sign the deed in front of two witnesses, as Florida law requires (s. 689.01).
  4. The buyer funds, the clerk records the deed, and you receive proceeds after payoffs.

Roughly 28.3 percent of Tampa residents use another language at home, so ask the closing agent for translated explanations or an interpreter if anyone signing would be more comfortable that way.

How is Tampa's housing stock split between owners and renters?

Half of Tampa households rent: 50.3% of homes are owner-lived, across 166,278 households of 2.31 people. Rent runs $1,701 at the median, and owners pay $2,179 a month with a mortgage or $640 without.

Investors are therefore active buyers. Residents are fairly young: 19.4% are under 18 and 13.7% are 65 or older, and 45.7% of adults have finished a four-year degree.

Tampa housing and income, Census QuickFacts
MeasureFigure

What should a Tampa seller know about storm damage and appraisals?

If your house took storm damage, ask the Hillsborough appraiser whether the 2026 Hurricane Damage Adjustment Form applies. Damage also affects sale options: lenders hesitate over open roof or structural problems, while cash buyers purchase as-is. Keep claim papers, estimates and photos together.

Who lives in Tampa, and where do they work?

Census data counts 19,465 veterans and 19.4% foreign-born residents. Two in three people 16 and older (66.1%) are in the labor force. Health care and related services took in about $9.65 billion in 2022, and retail sales were about $11.38 billion. Poverty stands at 15.5%.

That mix of military, health care, port and service jobs gives Tampa sellers a wide pool of buyers, from first-time owners to investors.

How do Hillsborough County property taxes work when I sell?

The Hillsborough County Property Appraiser sits on the 15th floor of 601 E. Kennedy Boulevard downtown, phone (813) 272-6100. Its site announced a 2026 Hurricane Damage Adjustment Form and a statement after Amendment 3 passed; read both before you list.

Non-homestead assessments rise no more than 10 percent a year, a cap that resets on sale (Department of Revenue). Many Tampa rentals fall in that group.

  • Homestead can cut assessed value by up to $50,000.
  • Renting the house can end homestead.

Which charges land on a Tampa seller at closing?

Plan for deed tax, recording fees, the seller's slice of the year's property tax and any payoffs. The deed rate is $0.70 per $100 here (Department of Revenue), and the clerk's fees are in s. 28.24.

What if I am a landlord selling a Tampa rental?

You can sell with the tenant in place. To clear the house, a nonpayment notice allows three days (s. 83.56). Never change locks or cut utilities yourself; the sheriff executes a court writ.

Can heirs sell a Tampa house?

Yes, after a personal representative has authority. Estates up to $150,000 outside exempt assets can use summary administration (s. 735.201). Bring the death certificate, any will and the newest tax bill.

How do I prepare a Tampa house for a quick sale?

Preparation costs little and speeds everything up.

  • Pull the deed, survey and latest tax bill.
  • Get payoff letters for every loan and lien.
  • Save storm and roof repair records and insurance claim numbers.
  • Gather leases and deposit records for a rental.
  • Clear personal items, since a cash buyer can see past clutter but needs access.

Ask each buyer for the offer in writing, including the closing date, who pays closing costs and what happens if an inspection finds a problem.

What does the Census say about Tampa's economy?

Tampa's 2022 receipts included about $2.92 billion in accommodation and food services and about $3.16 billion in transportation and warehousing, alongside health care and retail. Median household income is $75,475 and per capita income is $52,528, and 97.1% of households have a computer.

With 166,278 households and growth of 7.3% since 2020, demand for housing remains broad. A seller who needs speed can use that depth, since buyers range from owner-occupants to investors.

More questions about Tampa, FL

How soon can I close on a Tampa house?

Cash sales often close in days to weeks, depending on title. A clean title and a ready payoff letter are what shorten the timeline most, and a lien, a probate case or a tenant dispute stretches it.

Can I sell a Tampa house that needs a new roof?

Yes. Cash buyers take it as-is, with the price reflecting the work. Tell the buyer about leaks, past storm claims and unpermitted work so the offer stays firm through closing.

Does the buyer get my homestead tax cap?

No. The assessment resets to market level after the sale, so the buyer's first bill may look different from yours. Buyers can ask the Hillsborough appraiser about their own exemptions.

What does the Hillsborough County clerk charge to record a deed?

Statute sets $5.00 for page one and $4.00 for later pages, plus extra charges. Deed tax is billed separately.

Can I sell a Tampa house with a tenant in it?

Yes. The buyer takes the lease, or you end the tenancy by the statute's notice rules first. Collect the lease, rent ledger and deposit record to hand to the buyer.

Which sale route fits an Orlando house on a timeline?

Orlando sellers can accept a cash offer, hire an agent or sell directly, and the best fit turns on how much work the house needs and whether a historic district rule covers the address. Orlando had an estimated 333,888 residents in July 2025, and its housing stock ranges from downtown condos to bungalows built in the 1920s.

  • Cash offers suit houses with deferred repairs, tenant trouble or a tight deadline, since no lender stands between you and closing.
  • A traditional listing suits a house that shows well and can handle rounds of open houses.
  • A direct sale suits an owner with a buyer already in mind, perhaps a neighbor or the current tenant.

Before choosing, find out whether your street sits inside one of the city's six historic preservation districts, since a district limits what the next owner can do to the exterior.

How many Orlando homes are owner-occupied, and what do they cost?

Renters outnumber owners in Orlando: Census Bureau figures for 2020-2024 give owners only 39.5% of homes. Investors with rental plans are therefore regular bidders, and plenty of sellers own rentals themselves.

Census Bureau QuickFacts figures for Orlando city:

  • Resident count, mid-2025: 333,888
  • Growth since April 2020 base: 8.4%
  • Owner share of homes: 39.5%

The city covers more than 110 square miles, so values differ a great deal from one neighborhood to the next. Use the midpoint as a reference only, and get a price opinion for your own street.

How did Orlando's lakes and old neighborhoods take shape?

The city's own Lake Eola history says Jacob Summerlin bought 200 acres in what is now Downtown Orlando in 1873, and a sinkhole on the edge of the property filled into the lake first known as Sandy Beach. The Summerlin family donated land around the shore in 1883, and in 1888 Lake Eola became a public park.

The preservation districts tell the next chapter. Land north of the lake was planted in citrus until the freezes of 1894 and 1895 devastated the groves, after which it was subdivided for homes, and Lake Eola Heights grew most between 1905 and 1925. Colonialtown South was platted in part in 1883, and most of its houses went up during the 1920s land boom. Houses from those eras are common sale listings, and their age is why the local rules below matter.

Does a historic district change how I sell an Orlando house?

It can, since a house in one of Orlando's six local historic preservation overlay districts needs city approval before exterior changes. The city's Orlando Locator, which takes an address, shows whether you live in a district. Most districts require a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Historic Preservation Board, while the Downtown Historic District uses a Certificate of Appearance Approval from the Appearance Review Board.

Orlando local historic districts: designation year and review timing printed on the City of Orlando page
DistrictDesignatedQuick review for minor work
Downtown198010 to 15 days
Lake Cherokee19812 to 10 days
Lake Copeland19842 to 10 days
Lake Eola Heights19892 to 10 days
Lake Lawsona19942 to 10 days
Colonialtown South20002 to 10 days
  • Major work such as additions, new construction, relocation and demolition goes to a board hearing, and the city says to expect about seven weeks.
  • Lake Eola Heights does not require approval for landscaping, paint color, or patios and walkways out of public view.
  • In Lake Copeland, approval is not needed for work that needs no city building permit or for structures built after January 1, 1940.
  • Chain-link fencing is restricted in Lake Eola Heights and Lake Lawsona.

The city also reports that on August 10, 2026 the City Council approved a 36-month temporary change that moves reviews of new or renovated downtown projects from the Historic Preservation Board to the Appearance Review Board. For questions, the Historic Preservation Officer line is 407.246.3416, and Permitting is 407.246.2271.

Is there a tax break that stays with a historic Orlando house?

Yes, for rehabilitated historic property. Orlando adopted a property tax exemption in 1994 for the substantial rehabilitation of locally designated historic property. It runs 10 years and covers 100 percent of the city's share of the tax tied to the value added by the rehabilitation, and the city says the exemption stays intact when the property sells. If your house has had that work done, mention it in the listing and keep the paperwork for the buyer.

What happens to my homestead tax benefits when I sell?

Orange County's property appraiser says homestead can reduce taxable value by up to $50,000, and the office posts a tax estimator tool meant for people planning to buy or sell. Bills arrive each November, and paying that month earns the largest early-payment discount.

Your homestead ends at sale. The next owner files their own by March 1, and the property is reassessed at just value, a reset that follows any sale, foreclosure or transfer of title, with exceptions for spouses and certain transfers at death. Buying again in Florida? Portability can move part of your capped assessment to the new home if you establish it within three years.

Older owners and veterans may hold added breaks that the buyer will not inherit. A local ordinance can give people 65 and older an extra exemption of up to $50,000 within an income limit, and a veteran with a permanent service-connected disability may receive a discount matching the VA rating. Ask the property appraiser what applies to you.

Which closing charge hits the Orlando deed?

Florida stamps a deed at $0.70 for each $100 of consideration, and Orange County is among the counties on that standard rate. Everyone who signs the deed is liable no matter what the contract says about who pays, and the clerk gathers the tax as the instrument goes on record. Recording fees are separate and depend on page count, names and technology add-ons, so the closing agent's statement gives the real total.

What if a tenant is living in the house I am selling?

A tenant in place shapes your timeline. Florida requires 60 days' notice to end a year-to-year tenancy, and the sheriff gives 24 hours of posted notice before returning possession once a court rules for the landlord. Many investors buy occupied houses, so a lease is not always an obstacle.

More questions about Orlando, FL

How can I tell whether my address is in a historic district?

Enter your address in the Orlando Locator on the city's website, or call the city's Historic Preservation Officer at 407.246.3416. Six local districts exist: Downtown, Lake Cherokee, Lake Copeland, Lake Eola Heights, Lake Lawsona and Colonialtown South.

How long do Orlando's historic approvals run?

Minor work can clear a quick review in 2 to 10 days in most districts and 10 to 15 days downtown. Major work needs a board hearing, and the city says to expect about seven weeks from the closing date of the application.

Does my Save Our Homes cap pass to the buyer?

No. A sale is a change of ownership, so the county returns the property to just value. The buyer applies for a fresh homestead by March 1 if they live there on January 1.

What is the stamp tax on a deed in Orange County?

It is $0.70 per $100 of consideration, paid through the clerk at recording. Miami-Dade is the lone county with a different structure, and your closing agent can quote the exact amount.

Can an inherited Orlando house be sold quickly?

Often, once the estate has authority to sell. Florida offers a simplified summary administration for some smaller or older estates, and creditor claims have their own cutoff dates. A probate attorney can confirm which path your estate takes.

How much is a house worth in Port St. Lucie?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Port St. Lucie at $327,700.

Why is selling a house in Port St. Lucie different from most Treasure Coast sales?

Port St. Lucie is a very large, very young city in St. Lucie County. Its Census population estimate for July 2025 is 268,062, up 30.9 percent from the April 2020 base, and the city's own pages call it the largest city between Orlando and Miami and the sixth largest in Florida.

For a seller, that growth means plenty of nearby new construction and plenty of competition from similar houses. The city says it expects another 125,000 residents over the next 10 to 15 years, so buyers can compare your house with fresh builds. Sellers usually pick one of three routes.

  • An agent listing, which exposes the house to the widest set of buyers but invites repair requests.
  • A sale handled by the owner, which keeps costs low and shifts the paperwork to you.
  • A cash offer, which suits a house with deferred work, a vacancy or a short timeline.

How was Port St. Lucie laid out, and what does that mean for old lots and homes?

The city's Our Story page says Port St. Lucie was incorporated in 1961 by a development group whose goal was selling quarter-acre lots to retirees, without sidewalks, streetlights, water or sewer. Another city page says General Development Corporation turned 66 square miles into mostly single-family lots in the 1960s with little planning for commercial and employment centers.

Later growth reached St. Lucie West and land west of I-95, including Tradition, Southern Grove, Western Grove, Riverland and Wilson Groves. The city says the last Development of Regional Impact it approved came in 2007, and those owners hold entitlements to build.

That layout explains why many early lots were sold without sewer service. The city notes it runs one of the country's larger septic-to-sewer conversion projects, so ask the city utility about the sewer status of your street.

What do Census numbers show about homes in Port St. Lucie?

They show a city of homeowners, with 84.0 percent of homes lived in by their owners and 2.76 people per household. The city's own page also cites nearly 84 percent homeownership.

How do St. Lucie property taxes and Save Our Homes affect a sale here?

The city says it accounts for only 22 percent of a typical bill, with the county, school district, fire district and others making up the rest. The St. Lucie County Property Appraiser's FAQ says properties are reassessed each January 1, and that a buyer's exemptions and caps from the prior owner are removed, which can raise the bill.

Its answer on Save Our Homes explains the cap: annual increases on a homestead are limited to 3 percent or CPI, whichever is less, and the benefit starts to build only after the first year of homestead. The office lists January 1 through March 1 as the filing window for initial applications and renewals, and says homestead is not transferable to a new residence.

Voters approved Amendment 3 on November 3, 2026, according to another Florida appraiser's explainer, with a larger non-school homestead exemption from 2027. Ask the St. Lucie office how it applies to your parcel.

  • Bills go out in early November, with discounts of 4 percent in November, 3 in December, 2 in January and 1 in February.
  • Unpaid taxes become delinquent on April 1.
  • Ask the title agent to prorate the current-year bill at closing.

What is the Port District, and how does the riverfront affect nearby homes?

The Port District is a waterfront area along the North Fork of the St. Lucie River with parks, conservation areas, event space, trails, the Botanical Gardens, the History Museum and Pioneer Park. The city says the idea began over two decades ago, when about 2,000 feet of boardwalk was added north of Port St. Lucie Boulevard linking Veterans Park at Rivergate and Tom Hooper Park.

A public charrette at the Botanical Gardens in 2015 drew over 100 residents and led to a master plan that year, with a historic village, playground, event lawn, longer Riverwalk Boardwalk and riverfront dining. Funding came largely from the Parks Impact Fee, collected when new homes are built, plus state historic grants and Florida Inland Navigation District money.

If your house is a short drive from the river, mention the trail and park access in your description. Buyers compare these amenities with newer neighborhoods farther west.

What should a Port St. Lucie seller know about foreclosure timing?

In a judicial foreclosure the clerk sells the property 20 to 35 days after final judgment, unless the plaintiff agrees to longer, under section 45.031. The high bidder posts a 5 percent deposit and, if nobody objects within 10 days of the certificate of sale, the clerk files the certificate of title.

Homestead owners are told to check with the clerk within 10 days after sale about surplus funds. A sale that closes ahead of the auction date may keep more equity in your hands, so contact a lender or attorney as soon as a judgment issues.

The Department of Revenue says a certificate of title after foreclosure carries documentary stamp tax figured on the highest bid.

What deed and closing details apply in Port St. Lucie?

A deed in any Florida county but Miami-Dade carries documentary stamp tax of 70 cents per $100 of consideration, which includes any mortgage the buyer takes on. Every party to the document is liable, so the contract settles who pays, and the clerk collects it at recording.

Conveyances of land need two subscribing witnesses under section 689.01, and signing may be witnessed by audio-video technology.

  • Obtain payoff letters from each lender.
  • Check city records for open permits on sheds, pools, enclosures or additions.
  • Gather HOA or special-district statements if the neighborhood has them.

How do climate and nature shape a Port St. Lucie house?

The city lists average temperatures from 64 degrees in February to 82 degrees in August, and says the city lies about 50 miles north of West Palm Beach, halfway between Miami and Orlando. It also describes the North Fork of the St. Lucie River as a state-designated aquatic preserve.

Heat and humidity make air-conditioning age and roof condition major points in a buyer's inspection. Homes near the river or canals raise insurance and flood-zone questions, so keep your policy and any permit records for roof, window and enclosure work on hand.

More questions about Port St. Lucie, FL

Is a cash offer realistic for a Port St. Lucie house?

Yes, particularly for a house needing repairs or one with a time limit. A cash buyer skips lender appraisals, though title must be clear and the deed witnessed and recorded.

Does a buyer inherit my homestead exemption in Port St. Lucie?

No. The St. Lucie property appraiser says a buyer's assessment drops the prior owner's exemptions and caps, and homestead does not transfer to a new residence.

How long until a foreclosure sale after judgment?

The clerk sets it 20 to 35 days after final judgment under section 45.031, unless the plaintiff agrees to longer. Closing a sale first can protect equity.

Who pays documentary stamps on the deed?

The contract decides, though every party is liable under state rules. The rate is 70 cents per $100 outside Miami-Dade.

What share of my tax bill is the city's?

The city says it accounts for about 22 percent of a Port St. Lucie bill. The rest goes to the county, the school district, the fire district and other taxing bodies.

Selling a house in St. Petersburg FAQ

How much is a house worth in St. Petersburg?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in St. Petersburg at $331,500.

What makes selling a house in St. Petersburg different?

Waterfront geography, storm repairs and permit history decide how quickly a St. Petersburg house can close. The city occupies a peninsula in Pinellas County, and its website describes 244 miles of shoreline along Tampa Bay, Boca Ciega Bay, the Gulf of Mexico and intracoastal waterways.

That coast helps with pricing and complicates disclosure. Buyers, lenders and insurers ask whether the property lies in a flood hazard area, whether past storm damage was fixed under permit, and what the city has on file. Gather those answers early and you can say yes to a strong offer quickly, whether it comes from a listing or a cash buyer.

What does St. Petersburg look like for a home seller?

The city reports more than 265,000 residents across over 100 neighborhoods and calls itself one of the nation's fastest-growing cities. Its history page says the town of St. Petersburg incorporated on February 29, 1892, and re-incorporated as a city in 1903.

The city's own profile helps explain neighborhood demand:

  • A seven-mile preserved downtown waterfront and 137 parks and recreation areas.
  • The Pinellas Trail, a 54-mile route running coast to coast.
  • St Petersburg College, Eckerd College, USF St. Petersburg and Stetson University College of Law.
  • Averages of 74 degrees and 361 days of sunshine a year, per the city.

Proximity to the waterfront, the Pier and downtown arts venues can move prices block by block, so compare your house with sales from your own neighborhood rather than the citywide picture.

What should I check with the St. Petersburg building department?

Start with permit history and flood records, both held by the city's Construction Services and Permitting Division at the Municipal Services Center, One 4th St. N. The city says homeowners should get permits before repair, improvement or construction begins.

Florida House Bill 803, effective July 1, 2026, lets the city issue a Permit Exemption form for work on a single-family dwelling totaling less than $7,500. The city says this applies only outside flood hazard areas and does not cover structural components (including window, door, roofing, soffit and siding work), mechanical, electrical, plumbing or gas work.

City certificate types listed by the St. Petersburg permitting office

Elevation CertificateFEMA document showing height above sea level and base flood elevation; city records go back to 1990

The city also lets you research Certificate of Occupancy history for free in its property cards database. Pull yours before you list.

Bring a photo ID and a floor layout if you visit in person. The city also offers an optional preliminary plan review for proposed work, a useful step if a buyer wants to add to the house after closing.

How does flood and storm history affect a St. Petersburg sale?

If your house is in a flood hazard area and was damaged, the repair path matters to the sale. The city's permitting page points owners to FEMA's 49% Rule, which can affect a property after storm damage, and asks homeowners to bring photos, a damage summary and a floor layout when they visit.

The Pinellas County Property Appraiser notes a related tax effect: when a structure is damaged or destroyed, taxes can still rise for long-time homesteaded owners because of the Save Our Homes cap recapture rule. If the building value fell below land value, the assessed value may not drop.

  • Keep storm photos, adjuster reports and repair invoices together.
  • Locate any elevation certificate on file with the city for your address.
  • Confirm every repair that needed a permit has a final inspection.
  • Ask the buyer's insurer early about flood coverage, since it can change the closing timeline.

Cash buyers often purchase storm-damaged houses as they are, but expect a discount tied to the unknowns.

The Pinellas County Property Appraiser also advises owners with storm-damaged structures to read the value reconsideration letters they receive, since a building value can differ from the one used the year before.

How are Pinellas County property taxes handled when I sell?

The Pinellas County Property Appraiser values your home each January 1, and the Pinellas County Tax Collector sends the bill in November. A sale is a change of ownership, so the county says exemptions and caps the prior owner held come off on the next January 1, and the buyer's value resets toward market.

The homestead exemption of up to $50,000 requires a March 1 application. Florida's printed early-payment discount runs from 4 percent in November down to 1 percent in February. Ask your closing agent how the current year's taxes will be prorated.

If the buyer is moving from another Florida homestead, portability may carry over a savings cap. That is the buyer's application to file, within three years of January 1 of the year the earlier homestead was left.

What do deed and recording charges look like in St. Petersburg?

Pinellas deeds carry Florida documentary stamp tax at 70 cents on each $100 of consideration, which the clerk takes at recording. The Department of Revenue states that every party to the document is liable, regardless of the contract's allocation.

Recording itself costs $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 per added page under statute 28.24, with further per-page charges. A title company lists each item on the settlement statement.

Cash offers often skip lender steps like appraisals, which may shorten the schedule. Still, ask who covers title insurance, stamp tax and tax proration, and get the split in writing before accepting.

How do I verify contractors and open permits in St. Petersburg?

The city's permitting page tells homeowners to hire a licensed contractor and points to the Pinellas County Licensing Board for checking a contractor's license. It also says difficulty scheduling an inspection can come from an unknown license status, which shows how closely the system ties permits to licenses.

For work still in progress, the city's online portal lets you enter a permit number to schedule or cancel an inspection and check plan review status trade by trade. For e-plan submittals, applicants get ten business days to finish uploads or answer comments before the application is denied and the workflow ends.

  • Look up each contractor on the county licensing board's site.
  • Enter permit numbers in the city portal to see open reviews.
  • Call the permitting division at 727-893-7231 for license status questions.

A buyer's inspector will usually find stalled work, so settle it first or disclose it.

More questions about St. Petersburg, FL

Where do I get permit records for a St. Petersburg house?

Ask the city's Construction Services and Permitting Division at One 4th St. N. The city also offers a free property cards database for researching Certificate of Occupancy history, and its online portal tracks permit status.

Do small repairs in St. Petersburg need a permit?

Not always. Since July 1, 2026, a form lets the city exempt single-family work under $7,500 outside flood hazard areas, but not structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing or gas work. Confirm with the building department before starting.

Does my Save Our Homes cap go to the buyer?

No. A sale resets the assessment to just value on the next January 1, so the buyer's tax bill can be much higher than yours. The buyer can apply for a new homestead exemption by March 1.

Can I sell a storm-damaged house in St. Petersburg as is?

Yes. Many buyers purchase as-is, but disclose known damage and any unpermitted repairs. If your property is in a flood hazard area, ask the city about FEMA's 49% Rule before you decide to repair or sell.

More than 265,000 people, across over 100 distinct neighborhoods, according to the city's own profile page. Use the latest Census Bureau estimate if you need an official count.

Selling a house in Cape Coral FAQ

How much is a house worth in Cape Coral?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Cape Coral at $339,200.

What comes first when a Cape Coral owner decides to sell?

Sort out which Lee County office controls each piece of the paperwork, then weigh an agent listing, an owner-run sale and a straight cash purchase. Cape Coral homes are assessed, billed and recorded through Lee County, so the county's calendar and fees matter as much as anything the city does.

Valuation questions go to the Lee County Property Appraiser. The bill itself comes from the Lee County Tax Collector, and deed filing belongs to the Clerk. Start by pulling your parcel record and your latest tax bill so you know what a buyer will see.

  • Check that the owner names on title match the people who will sign.
  • Look for open permits, liens or unpaid taxes.
  • Ask whether a lender, a tenant or an heir has a say in the timing.

What calendar does the Lee County Property Appraiser publish?

The office lists a yearly cycle that starts with January 1 as the assessment date and ends with tax bills in November. It also notes that applications for exemptions filed after March 1 may be granted for the following year, which matters if you buy or move late in the year.

Lee County Property Appraiser, dates to remember
WhenEvent
January 1Date of assessment for all properties
January and FebruaryApplications for exemptions are filed for the current year
March 1Deadline for all exemptions and agricultural classification
April 1Tangible personal property returns due
July 1Assessment rolls go to the Department of Revenue

OctoberRolls certified for collection

The Property Appraiser also says owners may ask for an informal conference at any time during the year, which can settle a value question before it becomes an appeal.

How does the early-payment discount work in Lee County?

Early payers get a shrinking discount, starting at 4 percent in November and ending at 1 percent in February, per the Property Appraiser's calendar and the same state schedule used everywhere.

Delinquency starts April 1, and certificates go to auction by June 1. Under section 197.432 a certificate buyer waits two years before contacting the owner, and the tax deed application comes only after that wait.

The takeaway for sellers: settle the balance early, or let the closing agent pay from proceeds. An outstanding certificate can stall a buyer's lender.

What happens if the lender or the county is moving on the property?

Once a foreclosure judgment exists, time is short: section 45.031 sets the public sale 20 to 35 days out unless the plaintiff agrees otherwise. Notice runs for two consecutive weeks first.

Section 702.10 offers lenders a faster path, an order to show cause requested in a verified complaint. It also treats a home carrying a homestead exemption on the latest roll as owner-occupied unless rebutted.

  • Surplus funds: the judgment must carry a notice about them, and owners should contact the clerk promptly after the sale.
  • Tax deed sales: on homestead property the opening bid adds half of the latest assessed value.
  • If either process has started, call a Florida attorney first.

Can squatters or a lapsed tenant affect my Cape Coral sale?

Yes, an occupant can delay closing, but Florida gives owners real tools. Under section 82.036 an owner or agent can file a verified Complaint to Remove Persons Unlawfully Occupying Residential Real Property with the sheriff, who serves a notice to vacate and puts the owner back in possession when conditions are met.

Conditions include no tenancy, a non-family occupant, a property closed to the public, a request to leave and no pending lawsuit. A false statement exposes the owner to damages, up to triple the fair market rent.

Adverse possession is a different matter. Section 95.18 requires 7 years of actual continued possession under a claim of title, payment of taxes and a return filed with the Property Appraiser. A person who lives in a house only on an adverse possession claim before filing that return commits trespass under the statute. Most vacant-house problems never reach that stage, but a vacant property is the one to watch.

What should I gather before I ask for offers on a Cape Coral house?

Assemble a folder first. Buyers move faster, and offers come in cleaner, when the basic records are on the table. Most of these items cost nothing to collect.

  • Your latest Lee County tax bill and the parcel record from the Property Appraiser.
  • A recorded copy of your deed, which the Clerk can supply.
  • Mortgage and lien payoff information, plus any association or utility balances.
  • Permit records for additions, roofs, windows or other work done since you bought.
  • Receipts for major repairs, and any warranty papers you can transfer.

If a lender, a co-owner or a tenant is involved, note their names and contact details in the same folder. That way your closing agent can reach each person without waiting on you, and you avoid the delays that come from missing signatures late in the process.

Finally, decide in advance how low a price you would accept and how soon you need the money. Those two numbers make every offer easier to judge.

Which exemptions and relief programs might apply to a Cape Coral homeowner?

Several, and some depend on age or service. Seniors aged 65 and up may qualify for an added homestead break if a local ordinance provides it and household income is within the limit, under section 196.075. Veterans past 65 with a permanent service-connected disability may receive a discount equal to the VA disability percentage, and a disabled ex-servicemember may get a flat reduction in assessed value.

A tax deferral is another option, filed on Form DR-570 with the collector. Ask the Lee County offices which programs apply before you decide to sell under pressure.

What mistakes slow down a quick sale here?

Most delays come from paperwork that nobody checked early. A mismatch between the name on the deed and the name on a driver's license, an unreleased old mortgage, or a lien nobody remembered can add weeks.

Another common snag is timing around the exemption calendar. If you plan to buy again, remember that the January 1 assessment date and the March 1 filing date drive the new home's tax bill. Closing a week before or after those dates can change what you owe the next November. Ask your closing agent to flag which side of the dates your purchase falls on.

What goes on the closing statement for recording?

The deed tax uses the standard statewide rate in Lee County, since only Miami-Dade differs, and every party on the document stays liable even when the contract assigns the cost to one side.

Recording charges follow section 28.24 and run per page. Ask the Lee County Clerk for a total before closing.

A deed between spouses where the only consideration is a mortgage on the homestead, and divorce deeds for the marital home, fall under an exemption in section 201.02(7). A deed made for estate planning has no special exemption, per state guidance.

More questions about Cape Coral, FL

Which county handles Cape Coral property taxes?

Lee County. The Lee County Property Appraiser sets values, the Lee County Tax Collector mails bills in November, and the Clerk records deeds.

When is the Lee County exemption deadline?

March 1. The Property Appraiser's date list says filings after that day may be granted for the following year, so file as early as you can once you own the home on January 1.

How long can I contest my Cape Coral value?

25 days after TRIM notices go out in August. An informal conference with the office is available at any time during the year.

What if there are unpaid taxes when I sell?

Clear them for clean title, usually through the closing statement. Delinquency begins April 1 and certificate auctions follow by June 1.

Can I remove someone living in my vacant Cape Coral house?

Possibly, through a sheriff removal complaint if the statutory conditions are met, such as no tenancy and no litigation. If anything is in doubt, ask an attorney before filing.

What is Hialeah's story, and how does it affect a sale here?

Hialeah was incorporated in 1925, and the city marked its centennial in 2025. The centennial site traces the name to Muskogee words usually rendered as pretty prairie, and credits aviator Glenn Curtiss and Missouri cattleman James H. Bright with developing the area from 1921. Bright's company with Curtiss also built Miami Springs and Opa-locka.

Hialeah Park opened the same year as the city. It is on the National Register of Historic Places and is also an Audubon Bird Sanctuary. The park is a landmark inside the city, and the centennial site says visitors over the years included figures such as Harry Truman and Winston Churchill. In 1937 it was where Amelia Earhart said goodbye to the United States before her world flight attempt.

Who named Hialeah, and who built it?

According to the centennial site, James H. Bright, born in 1866, began buying Everglades land in 1909 and eventually held 120,000 acres, including the Bright Ranch near Hialeah. He and Chief Tigertail named the city. In 1916 Bright joined Glenn Curtiss to form the Curtiss and Bright Company, which developed Hialeah, Miami Springs and Opa-locka.

Curtiss, called the Fastest Man on Earth after a 1907 speed record, had left aviation in 1920 and moved to Florida. He built a home, an airport and a hotel in Miami Springs. Those neighboring cities share Hialeah's early story, and a buyer's agent may mention them when comparing nearby homes.

Which county bills Hialeah property taxes, and when are bills mailed?

Hialeah is in Miami-Dade County, and the Miami-Dade County Tax Collector sends the bill. The collector's page says the 2026 annual notices were mailed on October 30, 2026, and online payment opened the same day. The office is at 200 NW 2nd Avenue, Miami, and the phone number is 305-375-5448.

The collector does not set the tax. Value comes from the Property Appraiser, less exemptions, and the rate from each taxing authority. If the 2026 real estate taxes are not paid before June 1, 2027, a tax certificate may be issued, and the annual certificate sale starts June 1, 2027.

  • Water, road and sewer assessments, such as OJUS, are collected in annual installments, and a bill containing one must be paid by May 31 or a certificate is sold for the remaining lien balance.
  • Discounts for paying early step down each month, with the largest in November.

What did Amendment 3 change for a Hialeah homestead?

The Miami-Dade Property Appraiser's homestead page says voters approved Amendment 3 on November 3, 2026, and that it takes effect January 1, 2027. The change applies to non-school property taxes, and the school board exemption stays at $25,000.

The page notes that this provision depends on federal constitutional limits and implementing legislation, so a buyer coming from another state should ask the appraiser how the rules apply.

How do you file for, keep or lose homestead in Hialeah?

  • Renewal: homestead owners get a renewal receipt in late December, and no receipt goes to properties with a deed change.

Renting the house puts the exemption at risk. If the owner fails to report a change in status, the page says back taxes can reach ten years of exempted taxes, plus 15 percent interest per year and a penalty of 50 percent of the taxes exempted. Report any change before you list the house for rent or sale.

How does Miami-Dade's deed tax differ for a Hialeah seller?

Miami-Dade is the one county with its own rate. The Revenue Department lists 60 cents per $100 on a deed there, plus a 45 cent surtax per $100 that does not apply to a document transferring only a single-family dwelling. All other counties use 70 cents.

The clerk collects the tax at recording. All parties to the deed are liable, whoever the contract says will pay. The Department's list of taxable deeds names quit claim deeds and deeds in lieu of foreclosure, while a personal representative's deed under a probated will is not taxable. Use the Miami-Dade Clerk's current schedule to confirm the recording charges on your closing statement.

What should a Hialeah owner do about permits and inspections?

Ask the City of Hialeah building department for the permit history of your address, and pull any open or expired permit before you list. Items buyers often ask about are roofs, window replacements, electrical panels, additions and fences.

If the house has unpermitted work, a buyer may require the work to be permitted, repaired or priced in. A cash buyer may accept the house with open items, but a lender-financed buyer usually will not. Get the facts first, then choose the route.

What if you disagree with a Hialeah assessment or an exemption denial?

The state Revenue Department says a value challenge is a petition filed with the clerk within 25 days of the Notice of Proposed Property Taxes, and a denial of an exemption can be taken to the value adjustment board 30 days after the denial letter was mailed. The Miami-Dade appraiser mails the proposed notice by the end of August, and the page says the late-filing date shown on it is usually 25 days after mailing.

A sale is a good moment to check the parcel record. Confirm the owner name, the exemptions listed, and the mailing address on the tax roll with the Property Appraiser, so the notice reaches you.

Which ways of selling a Hialeah house are worth comparing?

  • Listing with an agent: wider exposure, more showings and inspection requests, and a closing that depends on the buyer's financing.
  • Selling to a cash buyer: a purchase in present condition, with timing you can agree on, and a price you should compare against a listing estimate.
  • Selling to a relative: still a taxable deed event, and it changes the property's assessment if the cap resets.

Whichever you choose, ask each buyer for written terms, the date money reaches you, and who pays recording and deed tax. Keep the Miami-Dade tax bill, any assessment notice and permit records with the contract.

What other Miami-Dade appraiser rules should a Hialeah seller know?

The appraiser's page says an owner who applies for homestead in another Florida county must cancel the Miami-Dade exemption, and that tracking an application is done through a status page. Suspected homestead fraud goes to an investigation unit at 305-375-3402.

The collector's page adds that BillExpress subscribers receive the annual notice by email on the mailing date. A deed change means no renewal receipt, so file a new application after buying.

Miami-Dade County, which means the Miami-Dade Tax Collector and Property Appraiser handle your tax bill and exemptions.

1925. The city celebrated its centennial in 2025.

March 1. A late application may still be taken until the date shown on the TRIM notice, and a $15 fee may apply.

Can I sell my house fast in Tallahassee, FL?

Yes, when the price is right and the paperwork is in order. A cash buyer removes the showings and lender steps, so a Tallahassee house can close on a timetable you set rather than a bank's.

Tallahassee is Florida's capital and the Leon County seat. Roughly 204,902 people live in the city by the 2025 estimate, 4.4% more than in 2020, spread over about 100.93 square miles of land. A house near the lakes and one near the campuses draw different buyers.

What shapes a Tallahassee house, from its hills to its history?

Leon County was created by the territorial legislature on December 29, 1824, and the city of Tallahassee followed in 1825, placed midway between St. Augustine and Pensacola. The city's own history page lists Florida State University's roots in the West Florida Seminary of 1851, Florida A&M in 1887 and Tallahassee Community College in 1966, which helps explain the rental demand in the Census numbers above.

The land is unusual for Florida. Tallahassee sits among rolling hills in the Big Bend, and the downtown ridge around the Capitol complex rises above 200 feet. The city grew by annexation, from 28.18 square miles in 1980 to 103.37 square miles at the end of 2016, so many addresses that feel rural are inside city limits.

How should a Tallahassee seller prepare the paperwork?

A short folder saves days at the title company, whichever route you pick.

  • The recorded deed, plus any survey or plat.
  • The most recent Leon County tax bill and proof of any exemption.
  • A payoff letter for each loan or lien.
  • Lease copies, deposit records and tenant contact details for a rental.
  • Roof, air conditioning and plumbing records, with receipts for any storm repairs.

With these in hand, a buyer can make a firm offer in one visit and the closing agent can start the title search immediately.

How do weather and trees affect a Tallahassee house?

Tallahassee's climate table lists about 63.5 inches of rain a year over 116 rainy days, 91 days above 90 degrees, and 35.7 days below freezing. Roofs, gutters and air conditioning units work hard here, and buyers look at all three during inspections.

  • Seven roads in Leon County, including Old Bainbridge, Meridian and Miccosukee, are designated canopied roads, which limits roadside development.
  • Large live oaks and other mature trees can overhang roofs and driveways, so expect questions about limbs and roots.
  • Summer humidity makes moisture, mold and HVAC condition standard inspection topics.

A seller who documents roof age, HVAC service and any storm repairs gives a buyer less to argue about.

What does the Tallahassee housing market look like in Census data?

Renters outnumber owners here. In the 2020 to 2024 data, 40.6% of homes are occupied by owners, and the city has 85,311 households averaging 2.16 people. Rent is $1,293 at the median, and the typical owned home is valued at $294,400.

Ask each buyer for the amount that will reach you after every cost, then compare it with a listing's net after commission and repairs.

What if my Tallahassee house has tenants in it?

A rented house can be sold with the tenant in place, and the lease goes to the buyer. To empty it first, Florida's statute gives a nonpayment tenant three days (s. 83.56), and a month-to-month tenant must get 30 days' notice before the end of a monthly period.

Collect the lease, the deposit figure and the rent ledger before asking for offers. Investors in a renter-heavy city like this one tend to value a paying tenant.

How do Leon County property taxes affect my sale?

The Leon County Property Appraiser sets values and exemptions, and the tax collector bills. The appraiser's own message says the 2026 bills were mailed in November and that Amendment 3 takes effect January 1, 2027, without touching 2026 bills. Call that office about how the amendment affects your situation while you plan your timeline.

Statewide, value is fixed each January 1, exemption claims close March 1, and delinquency starts April 1, with a November discount of 4 percent that shrinks monthly to 1 percent in February (Department of Revenue). At closing the title agent divides the year's bill by days of ownership.

  • Homestead can reduce assessed value by up to $50,000.
  • Renting the house out can end the homestead.
  • The new owner's assessment resets after a sale.

What closing taxes and fees come with a Tallahassee deed?

Deed tax runs $0.70 per $100 of price in Leon County, as in every county but Miami-Dade, and the state treats everyone on the deed as liable (Department of Revenue). The sale contract only allocates the cost.

The clerk collects it at recording. Page one costs $5.00 to record and later pages $4.00, with other per-page charges (s. 28.24). Request an itemized statement from the title company.

Can heirs sell a Tallahassee house they inherited?

Yes, once someone holds authority. That usually means a personal representative appointed by the Leon County probate court. A small estate that does not exceed $150,000 outside exempt assets, or where the death was over two years ago, can use summary administration (s. 735.201).

Florida levies no estate tax on deaths after 2004. Heirs should gather the death certificate, the will and the last tax bill before talking to buyers.

What happens if property taxes on a Tallahassee house go unpaid?

Unpaid Leon County tax first becomes a certificate sold to an investor, and a tax deed application cannot follow until two years after April 1 of the issue year. Owners who are behind should pay the certificate or sell, because a title company will not close over it.

Can a Tallahassee house be sold with a quitclaim deed or a family transfer?

Yes, but the deed form matters. Land deeds need two witnesses, and quitclaim deeds are taxable instruments. Changing names on a title shortly before a sale can reset the assessed value, so check with the title agent first.

Who buys houses in Tallahassee?

The Census snapshot shows 51.3% of adults age 25 and over with a bachelor's degree, 66.1% of people 16 and older in the labor force, and only 11.7% of residents age 65 or older. Median household income is $57,409 and 23.6% of residents are below the poverty line. The city's history page lists Florida State University, Florida A&M and Tallahassee Community College among its institutions.

For a seller, that means several buyer types: landlords, first-time buyers, and cash investors. Pricing a house near a campus differs from pricing one on the north side, so ask each buyer how they arrived at the number.

What is a realistic closing time in Tallahassee?

A cash sale can close in days to a few weeks once title is clear. A financed listing takes longer because of the appraisal and loan approval.

Do I need to make repairs before selling in Tallahassee?

No. An as-is sale leaves repairs to the buyer, and the offer reflects the condition. A listing buyer, by contrast, will often request repairs after inspection.

Who pays the deed tax on a Tallahassee sale?

The contract decides. All parties stay liable to the state either way.

Will my homestead exemption move with me?

Part of it can. Portability moves some assessment savings to a new Florida homestead if you set it up within three years.

What happens when a title problem turns up?

The title company must clear it before closing. Disclose known liens or heirs early.

Fort Lauderdale is the largest of Broward County's 31 municipalities, according to the city, and one of the ten largest cities in Florida. Every property has its own loose ends: a mortgage payoff, a tenant's lease or an estate that has not yet been opened. This page sets out the local facts and state rules that bear on each one.

How pricey is housing in Fort Lauderdale?

Fort Lauderdale's QuickFacts page estimates a July 2025 population of 188,677, a gain of 3.3 percent over the April 2020 base. For 2020 to 2024 it counts 80,999 households and shows an owner-occupied median value of $486,700, and 54.1 percent of units lived in by the people who own them.

Costs are high. Median monthly owner costs are $2,679 for owners paying a mortgage and $1,122 for those who are not, while the gross rent median is $1,854 and household income has a median of $83,130 in 2024 dollars.

Where does Fort Lauderdale's name come from?

The city takes its name from a Second Seminole War fort built on the New River in 1838, when Major William Lauderdale led Tennessee Volunteers south along the east coast. Three forts carried his name: one at the fork of the New River, one at Tarpon Bend and the largest on the beach at the site of Bahia Mar. None survive. Fort Lauderdale became a city on March 27, 1911, spanning roughly 36 square miles.

It counts about 165 miles of inland waterways, which earned the nickname Venice of America, and more than 3,000 hours of sun a year. Its economy now spans marine trades, manufacturing, finance, insurance, real estate, aerospace and film production.

Who lives in Fort Lauderdale and how does that shape buyers?

QuickFacts shows a varied population: 27.0 percent foreign-born, and 30.1 percent of residents over age 5 use a different language at home. 40.8 percent of adults 25 and up hold a four-year degree or higher, and 84.4 percent kept their address from the year before.

The mean commute is 26.1 minutes, and 91.8 percent of households have broadband. Working households with long local ties and many older residents shape the buyer pool.

The city points to the Riverwalk arts and science district, Las Olas Boulevard and a downtown that includes Broward College and Florida Atlantic University. Homes near them can suit buyers who want a short commute.

How does Broward County handle homestead after a Fort Lauderdale sale?

The Broward County Property Appraiser says all legal Florida residents may qualify for homestead on a home they make their permanent residence as of January 1. Its page reports that the basic exemption saved a Broward homeowner between $673 and $1,020 in 2026, depending on the city's millage rate, for homes valued at $75,000 or higher.

Deadlines are strict. The office states that the timely filing period for 2027 runs from March 3, 2026 through March 1, 2027, and that the last day to late file any 2027 exemption is September 20, 2027. It adds that state law bars late filing after that date regardless of good cause. For 2026, the timely deadline was March 2, and the late-filing deadline of September 18, 2026 has passed.

What should a Fort Lauderdale seller do about the March and September homestead dates?

Timing decides whether a buyer gets the exemption in the first year. The Broward appraiser stresses that state law bars late filing for any exemption after the September deadline, whatever the reason for missing it.

Pass these dates to your buyer at closing so the application is filed on time.

What if my Fort Lauderdale house has a tenant?

A tenant does not block a sale, but the notice rules for ending a tenancy still apply. Florida's chapter 83 sets short written notices for unpaid rent and for lease violations, and longer notices that depend on how often rent is paid, including a monthly-tenancy rule.

Ask whether the buyer will keep the tenant under the current lease, which avoids notice and court steps. If you need the tenant to leave, speak with a Florida landlord-tenant attorney before serving any notice.

What if I inherited a Fort Lauderdale house?

Most buyers want proof that someone has authority to sign for the estate. A smaller estate may qualify for summary administration, which is a streamlined court process, and creditors have a set period to file claims.

Florida has no estate tax for deaths after 2004, and a personal representative's deed under a probated will is not taxed for stamps. Ask the Broward County Clerk of Courts or a probate attorney which procedure fits your situation.

What paperwork do Broward sellers and new owners need for homestead?

The Broward County Property Appraiser asks applicants to bring proof of ownership, usually the recorded deed in the applicant's name, and notes that deeds already recorded in Broward's Official Records need not be copied. Where co-owners hold as tenants in common, every owner who lives there must file to claim full coverage.

For married couples and joint tenants with right of survivorship, any one owner may qualify for full coverage, though the office says it is advisable for all eligible owner-occupants to file. If the house is held in a trust, the office has separate requirements, so contact it before the sale.

Selling a house in Pembroke Pines FAQ

How much is a house worth in Pembroke Pines?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Pembroke Pines at $411,700.

Who is Pembroke Pines, and who buys homes here?

The city places itself in southwest Broward and reports more than 170,000 residents. It describes easy reach of major highways, jobs, parks and golf courses.

It was incorporated on January 16, 1960, when it was the Village of Pembroke Pines with about 1,500 residents. After Hurricane Andrew in 1992 the city's own history says it became the fastest growing city in the country, which is why so much housing dates from the 1990s and later.

Buyers here range from families drawn to its schools and parks to residents of the Century Village area. The city counts 41 arts and cultural facilities and describes its mission around raising a family.

How did Pembroke Pines grow, and what does that say about house age?

The area was open land and small communities, including the Pembroke Pines Country Club development, in the mid 20th century. Fire stations opened as the city expanded: Station 79 in 1981 in land annexed west of US 27 and Station 89 in 1986 at Century Village.

  • Land west of US 27 was annexed by 1981, so house age varies by side of town.
  • Check roof, electrical and plumbing age on your own house.
  • Ask a title agent what recorded items exist on your lot.

Knowing your home's age helps you decide whether a cash offer or listing fits. Six fire stations now serve the city, and in 2014 it joined the Broward County Regional 911 system.

What does Florida charge to transfer a Pembroke Pines house?

Broward is not Miami-Dade, so the deed rate is 70 cents per $100 of consideration. Each party to the document is liable.
