How did Kissimmee get its start?

Before it was Kissimmee, the spot was Allendale, a small trading post along the north shore of Lake Tohopekaliga. The city traces the current name to a modern spelling of a tribal word. After the Civil War a Philadelphia saw manufacturer named Hamilton Disston bought four million acres of marsh and plains for $1 million, and in January 1881 he contracted to drain the land and deepen the Kissimmee River.

Population rose past 2,700 by 1920, then an airport built in the 1940s by the Army Corps of Engineers lifted it by 38 percent to 3,700. Retirees followed in the 1950s. After Walt Disney World opened in 1971, the city went from 7,500 residents to 15,000 by 1980 and then to 30,000 by 1990. Osceola County, formed in 1887 from Orange and Brevard, is the 40th county in the state, and Kissimmee serves as the county seat.

Growth in bursts means houses of different vintages sit close together. A house from the 1950s and one from the 1990s wear differently. Jot down your build year, roof age and the last wiring and plumbing work before you collect offers.

What does Kissimmee code enforcement look for before a sale?

Kissimmee's code enforcement division handles over 5,000 cases a year. The guide makes the property owner answerable even when a tenant caused the problem, so settle anything open before a buyer looks.

The city's reference guide lists the common problems. Grass over 12 inches on an improved lot or vegetation over 18 inches on an unimproved lot, junk and trash, inoperable vehicles outside a garage, and cars parked on the lawn beyond two spaces beside the driveway are all violations. Cases left unresolved can reach the special magistrate, who sits in public on the second Monday of each month. If the city does the corrective work itself, it bills you and may record a lien when payment does not arrive.

The guide also says no work may start until a building permit is issued and posted where it is visible from the road. If you started a repair, finish or close the permit. Anyone renting a short-term dwelling in the city needs a business tax receipt from both Osceola County and the city, renewed each year by September 30, so a vacation rental house should have that paperwork current.

Other items in the guide that show up on inspection walks: a residential pool needs a barrier at least 48 inches tall with no gaps a small child could squeeze through, address numbers must be at least three inches high, and no more than five adult dogs and cats are allowed per household. A buyer's inspector will not care about the pets, but the pool barrier and street numbers are quick fixes worth doing before photographs.

  • Mow and clear debris.
  • Move inoperable vehicles into a garage.
  • Close out open permits.
  • Pull your business tax receipts if the house is rented short term.

How does Osceola County bill and collect property tax?

Osceola's tax collector opens collection each November 1, with the gross figure due the following March 31.

Pay in November for 4 percent off, December for 3, January for 2 and February for 1. April 1 is the delinquency date, when the collector's FAQ says 3 percent joins the gross amount. Escrowed loans work differently: the lender is supposed to ask for the bill, and you receive a copy.

The online certificate sale takes place by June 1. The collector stresses that a certificate is a first-priority lien and not a sale of land. A holder whose certificate sits unredeemed for two years may start a tax deed application, after which the clerk lists the parcel for an online auction. Redeeming on or after June 1 adds a $6.25 fee to the payoff. The county property appraiser's office, at 2505 E. Irlo Bronson Memorial Highway in Kissimmee, sets the value and handles homestead filings.

What happens to my homestead and tax savings when I sell?

Your exemption stays with you as an owner, not with the house, so a sale ends it on that address.

The state describes the exemption as up to $50,000 off value, with the first $25,000 reaching every taxing body and the second tranche reaching only non-school taxes. Save Our Homes caps yearly assessment growth at 3 percent or inflation, whichever is smaller, which is how a long-held house ends up assessed well under market. The next January 1 brings a fresh assessment at full just value.

Buying again in Florida? Portability can carry over part of the capped difference. The state sets a three-year window that counts from January 1 of the year you gave up the old homestead, and the filing date is March 1.

What does the deed cost and who signs it?

The deed tax here is the statewide 70 cents on each $100 of consideration, paid to the clerk at recording.

Revenue Department rules make every party to the deed liable, so who pays under the contract is a private arrangement between buyer and seller. Recording is billed per page, starting at $5.00 for the first. Florida requires two witnesses, and remote video witnessing is allowed.

Tenants in place bring notice clocks: a month-to-month tenancy ends on 30 days' written notice, and a nonpayment notice runs 3 days with weekends and court holidays left out. If a foreclosure is pending, the clerk's auction is set 20 to 35 days after final judgment unless the plaintiff allows longer, so a sale ahead of that date is what protects your equity.

More questions about Kissimmee, FL

Where is the Osceola County property appraiser's office?

It is at 2505 E. Irlo Bronson Memorial Highway in Kissimmee, according to the county's property appraiser page. The office offers record searches, sales transactions and map search. Homestead filings go there, with a March 1 deadline.

Does Kissimmee code enforcement follow a house after a sale?

Unresolved cases and recorded liens can remain on the parcel. Contact the city's code enforcement division for your address's status. The city's own guide says a lien can be filed if the city performs work and the bill is not paid.

Does renting the house short term need city paperwork?

The city's guide says anyone renting a short-term dwelling within city limits needs a business tax receipt from both Osceola County and the city, renewed each year by September 30. The building division can tell you what fits your address.

When does an Osceola tax certificate turn into a tax deed risk?

Two years after April 1 of the sale year, an unredeemed certificate's holder can apply. The clerk then sets an online auction. Paying off the certificate through the tax collector first ends it.

Can I sell if I inherited the house?

Yes once someone has authority to sign. Florida allows summary administration for small or older estates, and creditor claims are cut off on a fixed schedule. Ask a probate attorney which path fits.

Selling a house in Boynton Beach FAQ

How much is a house worth in Boynton Beach?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Boynton Beach at $312,700.

Which paths lead to a quick Boynton Beach closing?

Three routes exist for a Boynton Beach owner: engage a listing agent, find a buyer yourself, or accept a straight purchase from a company that pays cash and skips the repair list. Each route balances price against speed and against the work you do before closing.

Boynton Beach sits in Palm Beach County, which means three constitutional offices share the load: one values the house, one sends the bill, one files the deed. The city holds the building file for the house. Knowing which office holds which piece of paper saves a lot of calls once you have a buyer.

  • Agent listing: wide exposure, with showings, repair requests and a longer wait.
  • Do it yourself: you carry the marketing, contract and paperwork load.
  • Cash purchase: fewer steps and closing on a day you name, with the price reflecting condition.

What is Boynton Beach like for a seller?

Boynton Beach is a Palm Beach County city that began as a small settlement and became the Town of Boynton on April 14, 1920, according to the city library's history page. The same page lists a long run of mayors and charter changes, a reminder that the place has been reorganizing itself for a century.

Age is the practical point here. Older neighborhoods near downtown carry older construction, and buyers of older homes often ask for inspections and repair credits. The city keeps a permit history service that holds building plans, site plans, applications, certificates of occupancy and elevation certificates for properties inside its limits. Not sure what work was ever permitted at your address? Start with that file.

The same city page points anyone asking when a property was built to the Palm Beach County Property Appraiser. Pull that record early, since a buyer's agent will.

Which Palm Beach County offices do I deal with?

Three county offices matter. The Property Appraiser sets value and rules on exemptions; the Tax Collector mails bills; the Clerk handles the deed. The appraiser's yearly tax roll calendar is summarized below.

Palm Beach County tax roll calendar as printed by the Property Appraiser
Time of yearWhat happens
January 1All properties are valued as of this date
March 1Deadline to file for homestead and other exemptions, and agricultural classification
April 1Deadline for tangible personal property returns
May 1Deadline to submit income information for the limited-income senior exemption
July 1Preliminary roll submitted, denial notices mailed
Mid-AugustNotice of Proposed Taxes and Assessments mailed
Mid-SeptemberDeadline to appeal market values and denied portability applications to the Value Adjustment Board
NovemberTax bills mailed by the Tax Collector

Even a spring closing leaves the January valuation, and the exemption you held that morning, in charge of the bill that arrives in November.

Which transfer charges come with a Boynton Beach sale?

Florida's deed stamp rate, found in section 201.02, is seventy cents per hundred dollars of the sale price. Palm Beach County pays the common rate; only Miami-Dade is treated differently.

Liability reaches every party named on the instrument. The sales contract usually settles who actually pays, and the closing agent collects from that side. Price for this purpose includes cash, a debt that is forgiven and a mortgage that stays on the property, assumed or not.

  • Clerk recording charges under section 28.24: page one costs $5.00, later pages $4.00 each, and every name past four adds $1.00.
  • A records modernization charge and a technology charge per page sit on top.
  • Ask the Clerk's office for the current total on your document before closing.

The tax is taken at filing. A deed is taxable even if nobody records it, so one left in a drawer still owes it.

Why does the next owner's tax differ from mine?

Closing resets the assessment. Any sale, foreclosure or other title transfer is a change of ownership, which sends the property back to full just value in the next calendar year.

Two things follow for the seller. Savings built up under Save Our Homes travel with you only through portability, which needs a new Florida homestead within a three-year window and a portability form filed with that application by the March deadline. And your buyer should not expect your bill to carry over, because the new owner's first full-year figure can look quite different.

Renting the home out, or moving out for good, ends homestead. Avoid placing a tenant while you wait to close if the exemption matters to you.

How can I compare offers on a Boynton Beach house?

Line the offers up on net proceeds and on certainty, not on the headline number alone. A higher price that depends on a buyer's loan approval, an appraisal and a repair negotiation can end up worth less than a lower, firm cash figure that closes on a date you pick.

Ask each buyer to put their terms in writing and read them against the same checklist.

  • Who pays the deed stamp charge and the recording fees?
  • Does the offer hinge on financing or an inspection, and for how many days?
  • Does the buyer take the house with the current furniture, debris or tenants?
  • How many days does the buyer need between acceptance and closing?

A short list like this keeps you from comparing apples to oranges, and a title agent can estimate your net figure for each version before you sign.

How should I handle signing and recording the deed?

Section 689.01 says a conveyance of land must be written and signed with two witnesses watching. No seal is needed, and witnessing may happen through audio-video technology. Line up your witnesses and a notary with the closing agent early.

Once closing wraps up, the signed deed is filed with the Palm Beach County Clerk, who takes the stamp tax at filing. State revenue guidance lists warranty, special warranty, quit claim and trustee's deeds among the taxable instruments, so a quitclaim does not avoid the tax when money or a mortgage changes hands.

  • Confirm who signs, and whether anyone on title has died or moved away.
  • Collect payoff letters from any lender or lienholder.
  • Request a draft settlement statement from the closing agent ahead of signing.

What if the house needs repairs or has back taxes?

Selling as-is is allowed. Cash buyers build repair costs into the number, and you avoid contractors and open houses. Unpaid property tax goes delinquent on April 1, and certificates on those items are auctioned by June 1. Settle the balance at closing so the buyer gets clear title.

Qualifying homesteaders may also defer part of the tax. Form DR-570 is filed with the collector by March 31 following the assessment year. Palm Beach County's collector can tell you whether you qualify before you fix a closing date.

More questions about Boynton Beach, FL

Where do I find old permits for a Boynton Beach house?

The City of Boynton Beach keeps them. Its permit history service holds building plans, site plans, applications, certificates of occupancy and elevation certificates, and the city points to the Palm Beach County Property Appraiser for the year a property was built.

When must I file for homestead in Palm Beach County?

On March 1 of the year the exemption should start, pushed to the next business day only when it lands on a weekend, per the Property Appraiser. A buyer of your house files by the same date for the next roll.

Who covers the deed stamp charge here?

The sales contract decides, but every signer stays liable to the state. Palm Beach County uses the standard seventy-cent rate.

Do I keep my Save Our Homes savings if I buy again?

Partly, perhaps. Portability can move some of the benefit to a new Florida homestead, provided you set it up inside the three-year window and file the form by March 1.

What becomes of unpaid taxes at closing?

The closing agent pays them from your sale money so title passes clean. With delinquency starting April 1 and certificate sales by June 1, obtain a payoff number from the collector's office.

Selling a house in Doral FAQ

How much is a house worth in Doral?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Doral at $514,600.

Why does a quick sale work differently in Doral?

Doral is a Miami-Dade city, so the county's separate deed tax rate, its property appraiser and its tax collector apply to your sale. If your home belongs to an association, ask early about any payoff or approval it requires.

The city is small by area and dense with work. Its own About page puts Doral at 15 square miles with approximately 81,182 residents, and says more than 100,000 people work within the city. That workforce, close to Miami International Airport, keeps demand for housing steady.

  • List the house if you can wait for showings and lender timelines.
  • Sell as-is for cash if a move date, repairs or a tax deadline is pressing.
  • Ask your association about transfer fees, estoppel letters and approval steps early.

Where is Doral and how is it bounded?

Doral covers 15 square miles bounded on the west by the Ronald Reagan Turnpike, on the north by the Town of Medley, on the east by the Palmetto Expressway and on the south by the City of Sweetwater. It lies about one mile from Miami International Airport and twelve miles from Downtown Miami.

Doral location facts from the City of Doral About page
ItemAs printed by the city
IncorporatedJanuary 28, 2003
Land area15 square miles
West boundaryRonald Reagan Turnpike
East boundaryPalmetto Expressway
Distance to airportOne mile to Miami International
GovernmentMayor-Council-Manager

Source: City of Doral, About.

Highway access is a selling point for commuters, and it is worth naming in a listing or when talking to buyers.

How did Doral grow from swampland to a city?

In the late 1950s a couple bought 2,400 acres of swampland to build a golf course and hotel, opened the Doral Hotel and Country Club in 1962, and combined their first names to make the name Doral. The city's history page tells the rest.

By the early 1980s, Doral Estates and then Doral Park were built and named after the hotel. From 1983 to 1985 the county imposed a building moratorium to protect well fields, and growth surged once it lifted. Early residents lived with few stores, schools or parks and relied on low housing costs.

In January 2003, after a seven year effort, 85 percent of voters backed incorporation, and in June 92 percent accepted the charter. The city now describes development in areas such as Downtown Doral, City Place Doral and Midtown Doral. Newer buildings in those areas often sit in condominium or townhome associations, which affects how a sale closes. Read the full Doral history.

What does Miami-Dade charge on a Doral deed?

Miami-Dade uses its own documentary stamp rate: 60 cents per $100 plus a 45 cents per $100 surtax, as the state revenue agency prints it. The surtax is not due on a document transferring only a single-family dwelling.

That difference matters for a Doral seller. A single-family house avoids the surtax, while the agency's wording covers single-family dwellings only, so ask the closing agent how the surtax applies to a condo or townhome. Every party to the deed is liable no matter which side the contract assigns it to, and the clerk takes payment at recording.

The clerk's recording charge is separate and is set in section 28.24, with a first-page amount, a lower amount for later pages, and extra per-page charges.

When are Miami-Dade property taxes due for a Doral home?

Florida's calendar applies: the tax collector sends bills in November, discounts step down from 4 percent in November to 1 percent in February, and unpaid taxes become delinquent on April 1. Tax certificates are sold on unpaid items by June 1.

  • The property appraiser mails the TRIM notice each August, and a value challenge petition goes to the clerk within 25 days of that notice.
  • Homestead exemption applications are due March 1 on Form DR-501.
  • The Miami-Dade Property Appraiser lists exemptions, assessment reductions and land use classifications on its exemptions page.

Update your mailing address so a November bill reaches you after a sale. Ask the Miami-Dade Tax Collector for the current payoff before closing.

How can I weigh a quick sale against listing in Doral?

Compare net proceeds, time and certainty. A listing adds showings and a buyer's lender. A cash buyer removes the loan, but you should ask about association approval, who pays stamps and the closing date.

  1. Get a mortgage payoff statement.
  2. Request an HOA estoppel letter if applicable.
  3. Confirm the tax bill status.
  4. Ask each buyer for written terms.

If a foreclosure is pending, the clerk's public sale comes 20 to 35 days after final judgment unless the plaintiff agrees to longer.

How does Doral's government and history affect a seller?

Doral has run under a Mayor-Council-Manager form of government since incorporation, with a mayor and four council members elected at large. The council adopts the budget and appoints the city manager, clerk and attorney. City departments include Community Development, Public Works, Parks and Recreation, Finance and Police. Permit and code questions on your house go to Community Development.

The Doral Hotel and Country Club was the area's first structure. A spa was added in 1987, and the club later became Trump National Doral Golf Club after a 2012 purchase. Homes followed: Doral Estates, then Doral Park with a national builder, and many later communities took the hotel's name.

Early residents had to travel for basic goods because the area had no stores, schools or parks, and in 1989 the West Dade Federation of Homeowner Associations formed to resist unchecked growth. A Community Council was first elected in 1996. If your home is in an association, ask what estoppel or approval step it requires.

Ask the association for its transfer rules early. A buyer who must wait for a board decision can add days to a quick sale.

Can I carry my Save Our Homes benefit to a new Florida home?

Yes, through portability, if you establish the new homestead within three years of January 1 of the year you abandoned the old one. Forms DR-501 and DR-501T are due to the property appraiser by March 1.

The Department of Revenue's cap chart, revised January 2026, prints a 2.7 percent cap for 2026, 2.9 percent for 2025 and 3.0 percent for 2024. Homestead is lost if the unit is rented or stops being your permanent home. A deployed servicemember may rent out the homestead without abandoning it under section 196.061.

A condo owner who moves to another Florida county should ask the new county's appraiser how the benefit will apply.

What should Doral sellers check on the property record?

Start with the Miami-Dade Property Appraiser record for your folio. Confirm that the owner names match the deed, that the homestead exemption is on file if you live in the house, and that the mailing address is current so your tax bill finds you after the sale.

  • Look at which exemptions and assessment reductions the appraiser lists for your parcel.
  • Ask the association for any unpaid assessments, since those can follow the unit to closing.
  • Check city permits with Community Development if you did work on the house.
  • Confirm that the legal description on your deed matches the folio.

Confirm the municipality on your property record, since it decides which office handles permits and code questions.

More questions about Doral, FL

When did Doral become a city?

Doral was incorporated on January 28, 2003, as one of thirty-four municipalities in Miami-Dade County.

How big is Doral?

The city's About page lists 15 square miles and approximately 81,182 residents.

What is the Miami-Dade deed tax rate?

The state agency lists 60 cents per $100 plus a 45 cents per $100 surtax, and the surtax does not apply to a document that moves only a single-family home.

When do Miami-Dade property taxes become delinquent?

April 1, under the Florida tax calendar. Discounts run 4 percent in November down to 1 percent in February.

Does Doral have a building history that affects buyers?

Yes. The county imposed a building moratorium from 1983 to 1985 to protect well fields, and many neighborhoods began as Doral Estates and Doral Park.

Selling a house in Miami Beach FAQ

How much is a house worth in Miami Beach?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Miami Beach at $542,000.

How does Miami Beach's history shape a house sale today?

The city began as a barrier island joined to the mainland by the Collins Bridge, and it incorporated on March 26, 1915. Hotels, shopping streets and residential neighborhoods followed within a few decades, which is why a Miami Beach street can mix very different buildings.

The city's economic development writeup lists hospitality, retail, technology, healthcare, finance and the arts among its key sectors, and its rental and zoning rules are strict, as the rental section below shows.

  • Pricing: compare your house with sales of the same building type, not the whole city.
  • Rental rules: confirm what a buyer may legally do with the property.
  • Records: collect permits, association documents and insurance history.

What does QuickFacts say about housing and residents here?

The city's land area totals 7.69 square miles. Federal estimates for mid-2025 show 81,594 people, compared with 82,890 counted in 2020 and 87,779 in 2010, a slow slide over fifteen years.

The survey period 2020 to 2024 found 41,600 households averaging 1.95 people, and residents 65 and up make up 18.8 percent. About four in five residents (81.4 percent) were in the same home twelve months earlier. Households this small and this settled often sell because of an estate or a move to smaller quarters, and each of those has its own paperwork.

Table 1. Miami Beach by the numbers, Census Bureau, 2020 to 2024
ItemFigure
Median home value (owners' estimate)$556,700
Owner monthly cost, loan outstanding$3,256
Owner monthly cost, loan paid off$1,393

Even without a loan, owners carry $1,393 a month in taxes, insurance and upkeep. Keep that figure in mind if you are weighing how long to hold a vacant house.

Can a Miami Beach house be rented by the night?

No, not for a single-family house. The Resiliency Code, in sections 7.5.4.13(d)(E) and 7.5.4.11(a), bars rentals of less than six months and one day in all single-family homes and in many multi-family buildings in certain zoning districts.

Rentals that do qualify need a city Business Tax Receipt and a Resort Tax account. City code section 102-386 requires both numbers in every advertisement or listing. The city also publishes a list of apartment buildings authorized for short-term rental, grouped by zoning district.

A buyer who plans nightly stays will check these rules, and so should you. If your past income came from stays the code forbids, expect offers to be priced as a long-term rental or an owner-occupied home. Code Compliance and the city's Customer Service Center take reports of illegal rentals, and the city publishes a zoning map to check a property.

What does a Miami Beach seller pay at closing?

Miami-Dade is the one Florida county with its own deed stamp structure: 60 cents per $100, plus a 45 cents per $100 surtax that stays off a deed conveying only a single-family dwelling. Every other county charges 70 cents.

The base is the price plus any mortgage or lien on the property, whether the buyer assumes it or not. The clerk of court takes payment at the moment the deed is recorded.

  • Payoff letters for the mortgage, any home equity line and judgment liens.
  • Unpaid property tax for the year, prorated with the buyer.
  • For condos and co-ops, an estoppel or payoff letter from the association.
  • Title insurance and recording, as set out in the contract.

How do Miami-Dade property tax dates affect a Miami Beach sale?

Miami-Dade's property appraiser sets assessments, and the county's tax collector sends the bills. The appraiser states that its office neither mails bills nor sets or collects taxes. It certified the 2026 roll on October 16, 2026.

Florida bills arrive in November. The early-payment discount starts at 4 percent in November and drops a point each month through February. An unpaid bill turns delinquent after April 1.

Selling a homestead ends the exemption on that parcel, and the new owner is assessed at full market-based value from the next New Year's Day. A seller moving within Florida may carry over the saved amount by filing for portability along with the new homestead application by March 1.

What if the Miami Beach house is inherited or tenant-occupied?

No heir can deed the house until a court gives someone authority. Florida's short-form summary administration is open to small estates, up to $150,000 outside exempt property, and to deaths from over two years back.

A tenant complicates timing. A landlord can serve a 3-day written demand for unpaid rent, not counting weekends or court holidays, and a monthly tenancy ends on 30 days' notice. If the tenant stays past a court judgment, the sheriff posts a 24-hour notice before restoring possession.

Many buyers prefer a vacant house, so decide early whether you will deliver it empty or sell it with the lease in place. Put the choice, and the move-out date if there is one, into the contract. Keep every notice you served and every rent receipt, because a title company or buyer may ask to see them before closing.

What if the mortgage is past due?

Get the payoff amount and the court case status from your lender in writing. Once final judgment is entered, the clerk sets the sale roughly three to five weeks out, and the lender can agree to a later date.

A sale that pays the lender off before that date protects any equity you hold. After a foreclosure sale, the clerk is the contact for surplus funds.

Which Miami Beach records should I gather before listing?

Pull together the deed, your newest tax bill, any association documents and the insurance declarations page. Add permits for roofs, windows, air conditioning and electrical work, since buyers and their lenders tend to ask.

If the property has ever been rented short term, collect the Business Tax Receipt and Resort Tax paperwork. If it was never approved, say so plainly to buyers instead of letting an inspector or the city raise it first.

Miami-Dade's clerk offers a no-cost alert service that notifies an owner within a day if a deed or mortgage gets recorded under their name. It takes a few minutes to join.

How do I weigh a cash offer against listing here?

Subtract commission, repairs and holding costs from a realistic list price, then set the result next to the written cash figure. The offer should name who covers the stamp tax, the title policy and recording, and say what happens to a deposit.

Ask for the settlement date and the closing agent in writing, and keep a copy of every version of the contract. A cash buyer should be able to show proof of funds on request. If the buyer wants to assign the contract to someone else, ask who that person is before you commit.

More questions about Miami Beach, FL

When did Miami Beach become a city?

A city history article gives March 26, 1915 as the incorporation date, when the area was an undeveloped barrier island linked to the mainland by the Collins Bridge.

Can I rent my Miami Beach house for a weekend?

No for single-family homes. The city prohibits rentals of less than six months and one day there, and allows them only in certain multi-family buildings and zoning districts with a Business Tax Receipt and Resort Tax account.

How large is the city?

The Census Bureau puts its land area at 7.69 square miles and its April 2020 headcount at 82,890.

Is the deed tax in Miami Beach the same as in other counties?

No. Miami-Dade charges its own combination of 60 cents and a 45 cent surtax per hundred dollars, and a deed for just a single-family home skips the surtax; every other county uses 70 cents.

Will the buyer inherit my reduced homestead assessment?

No. The new owner starts at full assessed value after the next January 1. Some owners can carry the saved amount to their next Florida home.

Selling a house in Largo FAQ

How much is a house worth in Largo?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Largo at $208,500.

How can a Largo homeowner sell quickly?

The options are a cash sale, an agent listing and a sale you handle yourself. A cash buyer shortens the timeline because there is no loan approval and no appraisal gap to worry about.

Listing may bring more money from a financed buyer, though showings, inspection requests and a lender's schedule stretch the process. A house with an aging roof, code problems or an estate attached often moves better to a direct buyer. A well kept house with time on the clock deserves a listing opinion alongside any cash offer.

  • Compare offers by closing date and net proceeds.
  • Ask who covers title charges and deed tax.
  • Verify that no lien or tax balance will block the deed.

Why is the city called Largo?

Residents picked the name in 1886 while the Orange Belt Railroad was coming through, because a station needed a named stop. Some wanted Luluville, after the daughter of a prominent resident, but they chose Largo for the town's large lake, which the Cross Bayou Drainage District later drained completely.

The city says its central location and farmland made it the center of the area's citrus industry, which earned it the title Citrus City. Largo was incorporated in 1905, and in 1913 became the first town in Florida, and the second in the nation, to adopt a town manager form of government. A hard freeze late in the 1920s followed by the Depression forced the city back to its original 1905 boundaries as a town.

Population grew from about 1,500 in 1950 to over 5,300 a decade later. After a freeze in 1962, grove owners sold off land and builders put up homes, and by 1970 more than 22,000 people lived here. Today the city says it has over 80,000 residents and a base of medical, technology, manufacturing and hospitality employers. Before the freeze, groves surrounded the town, and Dansville was built to house the workers who picked and packed the fruit.

What neighborhoods and heritage sites shape Largo's housing?

Housing in Largo mostly reflects the postwar and post-freeze building years, with older pockets that trace back to the citrus era.

The city highlights Dansville, which grew from a 1946 purchase of 80 acres by Dan Henry in southwest Largo. He built a home for his family, invited other African American families to settle and provided housing for citrus workers. The city's history page also lists Heritage Village and the Largo Historical Society among local keepers of the archive.

The city names several local archives: the Largo Public Library, the Pinellas County African American History Museum and the Pinellas County Historic Preservation Board among them. If your house is old enough that its past could add interest, those are places to look for photographs or permit history.

For a seller, the takeaway is to know your build year and keep records of upgrades. A buyer's inspector will ask for the roof date and the age of the air conditioner and the electrical panel.

How does the Pinellas tax collector handle a Largo bill?

Bills go out on the last business day of October, payments are accepted from November 1, and April 1 starts delinquency.

The Pinellas County Property Appraiser sets values, and the tax collector mails and collects the bills. Up to two owners print on a bill, and address changes go through the appraiser, not the collector. If your mortgage company escrows your taxes, the notice you receive may be informational only. For the 2026 bills the collector lists the tax certificate sale as May 28, 2027.

Besides paying in full, the collector offers an installment plan for estimated bills over $100, with applications from November 1 through April 30. A partial payment plan takes payments of $100 or more but forfeits early discounts, and homestead owners may apply to defer taxes by March 31, which creates a lien and accrues interest.

Pinellas payment options from the tax collector
OptionTerms

Installment planFour payments, bill over $100, enroll November 1 to April 30
Partial payments$100 minimum, ends March 31, discounts forfeited

Source: Pinellas County Tax Collector property tax page.

What happens if a Largo property tax bill is not paid?

The sequence ends in a possible tax deed auction, and each step has a published deadline.

After April 1 interest and costs are added, and Florida law prohibits partial payments of delinquent real estate taxes. By June 1 the collector sells a tax certificate on the parcel, awarded to the bidder who accepts the lowest interest, with unsold certificates struck off to the county at 18 percent. After two years the holder can start a tax deed application, and the collector mails a warning letter each February to owners at risk, with a deadline of the last business day of March.

Once a deed action begins, all outstanding taxes roll into a single amount plus interest and costs, and only full payment stops it. Personal checks are not accepted for tax deed payments, only cash, wire or certified funds.

What else should a Largo seller know about taxes and deeds?

The deed carries Florida's 70 cents per $100 documentary stamp tax, collected by the clerk at recording.

The revenue department lists quitclaim deeds, deeds in lieu of foreclosure and contracts for deed among taxable documents, so a family transfer for value is not automatically exempt. A mortgage on the property counts as consideration. Recording is $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each additional page, and two witnesses must see the deed signed.

If you have rented the house to short-term guests, the Pinellas tax collector's FAQ describes a 6 percent tourist development tax on stays of six months or less, with a 7 percent state sales tax on top for a total of 13 percent. Returns are due even when no rent was collected, and a late return carries a $50 minimum penalty. Settle those accounts before you close.

  • Close or update your tourist tax account if you rent short term.
  • Collect lease copies for long-term tenants.
  • Ask the title company what it needs for the deed.

What about tenants or an inherited Largo house?

Tenants and estates both add timelines. Rental houses carry one more item: Pinellas taxes furniture and equipment in rental properties as tangible personal property, billed to whoever owns it on January 1, and any unpaid lien on it survives a sale of the property. Check that those accounts are paid.

A year-to-year tenancy ends on 60 days' notice, a quarter-to-quarter one on 30 and a week-to-week one on 7. A sheriff posts 24 hours' notice before returning possession after a court judgment. For an estate, Florida has had no state estate tax for people who died after 2004, and the personal representative no longer files the state forms.

More questions about Largo, FL

Which county is Largo in?

Pinellas County. The Pinellas County Property Appraiser sets values and the Pinellas County Tax Collector mails the bills.

When do Pinellas tax bills go out?

On the last business day of October, and payment is accepted from November 1. April 1 is the delinquency date.

Can I pay a Largo tax bill by credit card?

Yes, online, with a 2.50 percent convenience fee from the payment processor. eChecks are free. Delinquent taxes cannot be paid by personal check.

What stops a tax deed process?

Full payment of the rolled-up amount, with interest and costs, in cash, wire or certified funds. Installments do not stop it once the action has started.

What is Largo's tourist tax if I rented the house?

The Pinellas tax collector describes 6 percent tourist development tax on rentals of six months or less, plus 7 percent sales tax. Ask that office to close the account when you sell.

Lauderhill incorporated on June 20, 1959 with about 100 residents and now covers 8.5 square miles in Broward County. Its profile page gives a population of 74,479, a commission and city manager form of government with five elected commissioners, and zip codes 33311, 33313, 33319 and 33351.

Schools named on the profile include Broward Estates, Castle Hill, Larkdale, Paul Turner and Royal Palm elementaries, Lauderhill 6-12 STEM-MED Magnet School, Parkway Middle and Piper High School. Florida Medical Center is the hospital named there, and the page counts about 5,000 registered businesses with 10,475 people employed. The same page puts college-degree holders at 19 percent.

  • Confirm school assignment with the district before naming a school in a listing.
  • Mention the bus shuttle if your address is near a route.
  • State whether the house is single-family, a townhouse or part of an association.

Who signs the deed when a Lauderhill owner has died?

First settle who has legal authority to sign the deed. If the owner died holding the house alone, a court usually has to name a personal representative before a title company will close.

Florida allows summary administration for smaller estates, when countable assets stay at or under $150,000, and also once two years have gone by since death (s. 735.201). A house still counts as real property, so Lauderhill heirs normally need some court step. Creditors get a limited window: the later of three months from first publication of the notice to creditors or 30 days from service on a known creditor (s. 733.702).

  • Gather the death certificate, the will if there is one, and the deed.
  • Ask the Broward clerk what the probate division requires for a house.

Does an inheritance trigger state estate tax or a deed tax?

No estate tax applies. Florida's ended for deaths after December 31, 2004, and state revenue staff say filing Form DR-312 or DR-313 has been unnecessary since July 1, 2023.

Heirs often assume the closing costs are the same as in a normal sale, yet who owes what depends on how the transfer is structured and who signs. Ask the closing agent for a line-by-line estimate before the estate accepts any price, and keep that estimate with the estate records.

A personal representative's deed under a probated will sits on the state's not-taxable list for documentary stamps. An ordinary sale deed does not: it carries the documentary stamp rate stated in s. 201.02, seventy cents for every hundred dollars of price in Broward, and the signers share liability.

What happens to the homestead exemption and tax cap after a death or sale?

Both reset. Homestead depends on the owner living in the house as a permanent residence on January 1, and renting it out or moving away ends it.

Under Save Our Homes, yearly growth in assessed value stops at 3 percent or CPI, whichever is smaller, and the state's chart printed 2.7 percent for 2026. After a sale or other change of title, the following January 1 brings a fresh valuation at just value (s. 193.155). Heirs who keep and rent the house should expect a higher bill than the decedent's.

Neighborhood district meetings show which areas are organized and what is on the agenda, and sellers who attend or read the minutes learn what neighbors are asking the city to fix. For permits, code questions or a certificate of occupancy, call the city before pricing. Unpermitted work that a buyer discovers can slow a closing.

  • Keep receipts for repairs you complete before selling.

How should heirs compare offers on a Lauderhill house?

Put every offer on one sheet with the same lines: price, repairs the buyer expects you to make, who pays the deed tax, who pays recording, and the closing date. An offer that looks high can lose that lead once those lines are filled in.

Ask whether the buyer closes with no financing contingency, whether a deposit becomes non-refundable, and what happens if the estate needs extra weeks for court paperwork. A cash purchase tends to suit a house the heirs do not want to repair, with belongings inside and family out of state. A listing may bring a higher price when the house is clean and the estate can wait.

Photograph each room before anything leaves, and decide in writing who gets which keepsakes. Disagreements among heirs can stall a closing as surely as a missing document can. Name one heir to speak with buyers and the title company, so that every question gets a single answer.

How should I clear and prepare an inherited house?

Plan the work in a weekend or two. Walk through with a list and sort contents into keep, donate, sell and discard piles. Keep personal papers, tax returns, insurance policies and anything with an account number in a locked box until the estate attorney says what to retain.

Check that utilities stay on, the locks are changed, and the insurer knows the owner has died, since a vacant house can change coverage terms. Mow, remove mail and flyers, and photograph the condition so you can show what the buyer saw.

If the house needs work and no heir wants to manage contractors, an as-is sale shifts that job to the buyer. Get the price in writing and compare it to what a repaired house might bring after months of effort and carrying costs.

Can heirs sell before the estate closes?

Does Florida charge estate tax on a house passed to heirs?

No. The state tax ended for deaths after December 31, 2004.

What is the Save Our Homes cap in 2026?

Who pays the deed tax when a Lauderhill house sells?

The signers share liability whichever party the contract names, at seventy cents on each hundred dollars of price in Broward (s. 201.02).

Which schools does the city profile name?

What should a St. Cloud seller prepare first?

St. Cloud sellers should start with permit records, because the city's building department regulates a long list of home work and buyers ask for proof. St. Cloud is in Osceola County on the shore of East Lake Tohopekaliga, and it is one of the county's two main cities along with Kissimmee.

A quick sale goes best when three things are ready: the deed, the permits for any roof, window, pool or air conditioning work, and a clear idea of the tax bill. Gather those before you talk to any buyer, whether it is an agent, a private buyer or a company offering cash.

How did St. Cloud begin?

Osceola County's history page says St. Cloud was founded on East Lake Tohopekaliga in 1909 and was incorporated in 1911. It earned the nickname Soldier City as an early home to the largest concentration of Union Army veterans in the South.

The same page says the city drew those veterans with inexpensive city lots, nearby farmland and a climate with no extremes. Osceola County itself was carved from Orange and Brevard counties in 1887 and was a hub for riverboats, railroads, cattle, sugar and lumber.

Buyers still pay attention to the lake setting and to the distance from Kissimmee and the rest of the county.

What permits does the City of St. Cloud require?

The city says a permit is often required before starting a project, and its building department works under the 8th Edition of the Florida Building Code. The city lists the ultimate design wind speed for St. Cloud as 140 MPH for Risk Category II buildings.

The city's building department notes that St. Cloud falls under a 140 MPH ultimate design wind speed for Risk Category II buildings. For a house, that means roofs, window and door units, shutters and screen enclosures are inspected against a wind standard, and replacements need permits.

Buyers, insurers and inspectors ask about those items first. If your roof or windows were replaced, locate the permit number and final inspection. If emergency repairs had to be done quickly, the city says the permit application is due by the next working business day, so check that a late permit did not slip through.

How are Osceola County property taxes handled in a St. Cloud sale?

The Osceola County property appraiser sets value each January 1, and the tax collector mails bills in November. Under Save Our Homes, a sale resets a capped assessment to just value on the next January 1, so the buyer's bill may exceed yours.

The homestead exemption of up to $50,000 comes by application to the property appraiser by March 1, and the owner must live there as a permanent residence by January 1. Notices of proposed taxes arrive in August. A value challenge goes to the clerk of the court within 25 days of that notice. Ask the Osceola County property appraiser about exemptions on your parcel, and ask your closing agent how the year's bill will be split.

What do stamp tax and recording cost on a St. Cloud deed?

Florida taxes the deed at 70 cents per $100 of consideration, and the Osceola County clerk collects that tax as the deed is recorded. The Department of Revenue makes every party on the document liable, whichever side the contract names.

Per-page clerk fees come from section 28.24, opening at $5.00 and then $4.00 a page, plus smaller charges per page. Your title agent will itemize all of it.

Before agreeing to a cash offer, ask who pays stamp tax, title insurance and recording, and how many days the buyer needs.

Which offices handle a St. Cloud sale?

Three county offices touch a St. Cloud sale, and each has a distinct job. The property appraiser sets just value every January 1, mails the August notice of proposed taxes and decides who qualifies for exemptions. The tax collector sends the November bill, takes payment and handles deferral and installment requests. The clerk of the circuit court records your deed and collects the stamp tax.

  • If you disagree with your value, file a petition with the clerk within 25 days of the August notice.
  • If an exemption or classification was denied, petition the value adjustment board within 30 days of the denial letter's mailing.
  • Pre-sale, ask the tax collector for a payoff of any balance so the closing agent can settle it.

Those deadlines recur every year, so an appeal made after a sale is possible only for the tax year still open.

What about sheds, accessory units and manufactured homes in St. Cloud?

The city's permit list names accessory dwelling units, sheds, gazebos, carports, garages, docks, flagpoles and manufactured or modular structures among regulated work. A backyard structure that was never permitted is a common surprise during a buyer's review.

If you have one, ask the city building department how it was classified and what a retroactive permit would require. The city also says siding or soffit work covering more than 25 percent of a structure needs a permit, while smaller repairs on wood siding and stucco over block are listed as not needing one. Cash buyers can often take an unpermitted shed or carport in stride, but it may shape their price.

Does the City of St. Cloud need to approve a roof replacement?

Yes. The city lists reroofing as work that requires a building permit. Keep the permit and final inspection records, since buyers and insurers often ask for them.

What is the nickname for St. Cloud?

Soldier City. Osceola County says the nickname came from the large number of Union Army veterans who settled there after the city was founded in 1909.

Can I paint or replace carpet without a permit in St. Cloud?

Yes. The city lists painting, carpeting, cabinets and gutters among work that does not need a building permit. Confirm unusual projects with the building department.

Does the buyer keep my homestead cap?

No. A sale is a change of ownership, so the assessment resets to just value on the next January 1. The buyer must apply for their own homestead exemption by March 1.

How can I pay St. Cloud permit fees?

Not in cash. The city stopped accepting cash payments on January 1, 2025, and says staff can explain the alternative payment methods.

How can a Tamarac owner sell quickly?

Pick the route that matches your deadline: a listing for the widest market, an as-is investor sale for speed, or a cash offer when you want the fewest steps. Tamarac is a compact Broward County city, and a tidy plan for paperwork matters as much as the buyer you choose.

Tamarac holds an estimated 74,134 people on 11.59 square miles of land, and the 2020 count came to 6,205.5 residents per square mile. With that density, most sales here are condos, villas and single-family houses on small lots, and buyers compare them closely.

Where did Tamarac's neighborhoods come from?

Tamarac was incorporated on July 19, 1963 by developer Kenneth E. Behring, who set out to give active retirees something between a condominium and a single-family home. The first neighborhood, Tamarac Lakes on the east side, had one-story homes with one or two bedrooms around a shared clubhouse, and residents paid a small monthly fee covering lawn care, periodic painting and roof cleaning.

Mainlands and Woodlands came next as the company bought more land, and that piecemeal buying is why the city has an odd outline. How do veterans and snowbirds figure into Tamarac sales?

Commutes are long in Tamarac: the average trip to work is 31.4 minutes. The labor force participation rate is 62.5%, and 12.4% of residents under 65 have no health insurance. Median household income is $61,718, and 13.0% of residents are in poverty.

How crowded is Tamarac compared with a decade ago?

Steady growth on fixed land means competition for homes, and sellers can point to it. Still, an offer is only worth its net, so compare terms.

How does Broward County property tax work for a Tamarac seller?

The Broward County Property Appraiser sets values and exemptions, and its office answers at 954-357-6830 on weekdays from 8 am to 5 pm. A buyer does not inherit your capped assessment, since a change of ownership resets it the next January 1.

A homestead cap keeps annual growth to the lower of 3 percent or CPI (Department of Revenue), which is why a long-held Tamarac house can carry a bill far under a new owner's. The calendar is on the state tax page.

Can I keep my Save Our Homes benefit if I move within Florida?

Part of it, through portability. Set up the next homestead within three years of January 1 of the year you left this one, and file Form DR-501T with the DR-501 by March 1 (guide). The clock starts from the January 1 date, not the closing.

What if a Tamarac owner has died or the house is inherited?

A personal representative must be named before a sale, unless the estate fits summary administration (s. 735.201). Lady bird deeds are a different tool, and the Department of Revenue has advised that one such deed carried no stamp tax on its facts. Have a Florida attorney read your deed.

What if I owe more than the house is worth in Tamarac?

Speak to the lender early. Selling before a court sale lets you choose the buyer and the date. Foreclosure sales follow judgment within 20 to 35 days unless extended (s. 45.031).

How do I choose between a cash buyer and a listing?

Compare net proceeds, timeline and risk.

Older owners can defer part of a homestead bill by filing Form DR-570 with the tax collector by March 31, and installment plans need an application by May 1 (calendar). Deferred tax is repaid at sale, so request a payoff figure early.

Can I sell a Tamarac house with a quitclaim deed or two owners?

Land deeds need two witnesses, and every owner must sign. Settle any missing signature before the closing date.

What should a Tamarac seller do first this week?

  4. Two or three buyers, for written offers you can compare.

Doing these in one week gives you a full picture of the net you can expect, and it keeps any deadline from sneaking up on you.

Selling in Ocala?

Selling a house in Ocala FAQ

How much is a house worth in Ocala?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Ocala at $219,900.

What are the quickest ways to move an Ocala house?

Three routes move an Ocala house fast: a cash purchase, an agent listing at a sharp price, or a direct sale to someone you already know. Ocala serves as Marion County's seat, and the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 estimate puts owner-occupancy at 52.1% of the city's homes, with the rest rented.

  • Cash purchase: no lender appraisal to wait on, so the closing date is mostly yours to set, and the house changes hands as it stands.
  • Agent listing: the widest audience, paid for with showings, repair negotiations and a commission.
  • Direct sale: you keep the whole price and write the paperwork yourself, so a title company usually handles the closing.

Older Ocala houses add a wrinkle, because some sit in locally regulated historic districts, and a seller who knows that early can price and negotiate with it in mind.

Who lives in Ocala, and what do homes cost to own?

Census Bureau QuickFacts counts an estimated 71,753 Ocala residents in July 2025, 12.7% more than the 2020 estimates base. The typical household has 2.34 members, retirees past 65 make up 19.8% of the population, and 84.2% of residents stayed put over the last year.

Ocala city, Florida: Census Bureau QuickFacts (2020-2024 survey unless noted)
MeasureFigure

Treat the home value as a citywide midpoint. Street, lot size and condition decide where one particular Ocala house lands, and a broker's price opinion or an appraisal gives a sharper number.

Why do people call Ocala the Brick City?

A Thanksgiving Day fire in 1883 wiped out the center of town, and rebuilding in brick and other fire-resistant materials gave Ocala the name it still carries. The city's history page links the place name to Ocali, a Timucuan village, and says the settlement grew because Fort King played a strategic role during the American Indian Wars.

  • 1846: Ocala becomes seat of the newly formed Marion County, named for General Francis Marion.
  • 1858: the town is one of the leading business and social centers in Florida.
  • Civil War years: business collapses and the population falls to roughly 200.
  • 1880: Joseph Caldwell plats a 50-block area southeast of the original plat, on land from the 1817 Alvarez grant.
  • 1890: four square miles and 1,895 residents, the fifth largest town in the state.

The oldest houses stand within a few blocks of the courthouse square, which is why they now belong to the Ocala and Tuscawilla Park Historic Districts.

Does a historic district limit what a buyer can do with my house?

If the house is inside the Ocala or Tuscawilla Park district, yes: exterior work needs a Certificate of Appropriateness first. Ocala lists four historic districts. Those two are local and national, while Downtown Commercial and West Ocala hold only a national listing, so the local review covers just the first pair.

Applicants file through the city's eTRAKiT portal a full month ahead of the Historic Preservation Advisory Board meeting. The city charges nothing to apply. The packet includes a signed form, manufacturer specifications and drawings for windows, doors, siding, roofing and fencing, a site plan if relevant, proof of ownership and, for new construction, plans no larger than 11 by 17 inches showing all four elevations. The board generally gathers on the first Thursday of each month at four in the afternoon in City Hall, 110 SE Watula Ave.

Two consequences stand out for sellers. The certificate comes before any other permit, and a building permit pulled without one is invalid. Work done without approval can draw fines under the city code. Email historic@ocalafl.org with your address if you are unsure whether it is covered, and tell any buyer who plans exterior changes.

What happens with the property tax bill when an Ocala house sells?

The owner on January 1 is the one assessed for the year, so the bill that arrives in November is split at closing. Marion County's property appraiser sets value and exemptions, with exemption applications due March 1. The tax collector then bills and collects, and the discount starts at 4 percent for November payment before falling by a point each month through February.

Bills left unpaid turn delinquent April 1, and certificates go to auction by June 1. For you, the practical step is to read the proration line in the settlement statement.

Save Our Homes limits how fast a homestead's assessment can climb, and the state's chart shows the 2026 limit at 2.7 percent. That protection stays with the owner, so after a sale the county reassesses the house at full just value, and your own exemption lapses when you move out.

What does Florida charge on the Ocala deed?

Section 201.02 puts documentary stamp tax at 70 cents on every $100 of consideration, and mortgages or encumbrances on the land count as consideration whether or not the buyer takes them on. Every signer is liable to the state however the contract allocates the cost, and the clerk collects at recording. Recording adds page-based fees, starting at five dollars for the first page, along with surcharges for extra names and technology.

What if foreclosure or a tax deed is on the horizon?

After a final foreclosure judgment, the clerk auctions the property between 20 and 35 days out unless the plaintiff agrees to wait. A 5 percent deposit is due from the winning bid, and an objection window of 10 days follows the certificate of sale. Homestead owners entitled to surplus are told to contact the clerk within those 10 days.

A tax deed is slower. The certificate holder may apply two years after April 1 of the issue year, and a homestead opens at the amounts owed plus half its latest assessed value. Bring any notice to a lawyer before signing an offer.

Which steps should come first before I accept an Ocala offer?

  • Find out from city staff whether your parcel sits in the Ocala or Tuscawilla Park local district.
  • Gather payoff letters from each lender or lienholder.
  • Check last year's bill for a homestead exemption and any special line items.
  • Compare offers by what lands in your account after the deed tax and recording fees.
  • Ask the closing agent to explain the proration of the year's property tax.

Keep copies of the payoff letters, the latest tax bill and any historic approval paperwork together, because a title company and the buyer will each ask for them during the closing.

More questions about Ocala, FL

Can an Ocala house in poor repair still sell?

Yes. Cash buyers and investors take houses in rough shape, and conventional buyers can negotiate credits. Inside the Ocala or Tuscawilla Park district, though, any exterior fix needs the historic approval first.

Is there a fee to apply for a Certificate of Appropriateness in Ocala?

No. The city lists no application fee. Submit through eTRAKiT a month before the board meets, since the certificate must be in hand before any other permit.

Will my Marion County homestead exemption pass to the buyer?

No. It ends when you stop living there, and the buyer files their own by March 1 if the house is their home on January 1. After the sale the county reassesses at full just value.

When does the 4 percent discount on a Marion County tax bill apply?

It applies to payment in November, when bills go out. The discount drops to 3 percent in December, 2 in January and 1 in February. Delinquency starts April 1.

How do I sell a house I inherited in Ocala?

Start with the probate route. A probate lawyer can say whether summary administration, which Florida reserves for smaller or older estates, fits your case.

How much is a house worth in Delray Beach?

Delray Beach is a Palm Beach County city, so your tax bill, deed recording and tax-certificate rules come from county offices. A fast sale here usually depends on three items: how the house looks and works, any mortgage payoff, and the property tax calendar.

The city's own history page describes a place that grew from a small farming village to a city of nearly 70,000 residents, with a historic downtown on Atlantic Avenue and older neighborhoods around it. Older homes near downtown can carry deferred maintenance, while newer ones elsewhere in the city tend to need less. Buyers who use mortgages may ask for repairs. Cash buyers often buy as-is.

  • List the house with an agent if you can wait for showings and a lender's timeline.
  • Sell as-is for cash if repairs, a move date or a tax deadline is pressing.

How did Delray Beach get its name and shape?

The town was first called Linton, then Delray, and finally Delray Beach after a merger of two municipalities in 1927. The city's timeline traces each step.

Delray Beach name and incorporation timeline from the City of Delray Beach
YearWhat happened
1895Plat of the Town of Linton drawn; Atlantic Avenue platted
1896Florida East Coast Railway completed through town

Source: City of Delray Beach, About Delray Beach.

The split between the mainland and the barrier island explains why Delray still has two distinct feels, a beachside area east of the waterway and inland neighborhoods to the west. The first bridge over the canal was built in 1911 to link them.

Which Delray Beach landmarks affect how a house sells?

Old School Square and Atlantic Avenue anchor the downtown, and houses within walking distance often draw buyers who want that setting. The 1913 school building now houses the Cornell Museum of Art and History, and the 1925 high school building is the Crest Theatre. The city says the Old School Square campus was revitalized in the 1990s.

The city also lists three All-America City awards, in 1993, 2001 and 2017, and says it was the first city in Florida to win it three times. Those details are part of why buyers look at older blocks near downtown.

If your home is in or near a historic area, ask the city's planning staff about any rules for exterior changes before a buyer commits to a renovation plan. A renovation buyer will want to know that early.

When are Palm Beach County property taxes due for a Delray Beach house?

The county tax collector mails more than 600,000 property tax bills by November 1, and they are payable from November 1 through March 31. Property tax turns delinquent on April 1 and then carries penalties and interest.

The Palm Beach County Tax Collector's discount schedule is 4 percent in November, 3 percent in December, 2 percent in January and 1 percent in February, with no discount in March. Florida law pushes a weekend or holiday deadline to the next working day, as the county notes.

  • The property appraiser mails the Notice of Proposed Taxes each August.
  • Delinquent tax cannot be paid online, and the office says postmark date is not proof of payment once the tax is delinquent.
  • If you sold the house and the bill still came to you, the tax collector has a Property Sold Form so the bill can be redirected.

The county's property tax page also lists an installment plan and a homestead tax deferral. Ask the office whether you qualify before you list the house.

What does Florida charge on a Delray Beach deed and recording?

The deed tax in section 201.02 is 70 cents on every $100 of consideration, and all parties on the deed are liable whichever one agrees to pay. Palm Beach County is not Miami-Dade, so the ordinary statewide rate applies.

Section 28.24 lets the clerk bill $5.00 on page one and $4.00 per page after it, with trust fund and technology charges on top. Spousal homestead deeds where the only consideration is a mortgage, and divorce deeds for the marital home, are listed as exempt.

Lady bird deeds are sometimes used by older owners. A Department of Revenue advisement from October 2020 concluded that one on the facts presented was not subject to documentary stamp tax because the life tenants kept full powers, but it is specific to those facts. Ask a title attorney before relying on it.

How do I choose between a listing and a quick sale in Delray Beach?

Compare the net amount, the time to close and the risk that a deal falls through. A listing can reach more buyers but adds showings, appraisal and loan conditions. Cash can close on your date and tends to skip repair demands.

  1. Get your mortgage payoff in writing.
  2. Check whether property taxes for the current year are paid.
  3. Ask each buyer who pays stamps, title and recording.
  4. Ask for the closing statement ahead of time.

If a foreclosure is pending, remember that the clerk's sale follows final judgment within 20 to 35 days unless the plaintiff agrees to more time.

What does Delray Beach's farming and railroad past mean for older neighborhoods?

Delray Beach grew around farms, a railroad and a beach, and older blocks reflect each layer. The city's timeline notes that the Orange Grove House of Refuge, built in 1876 by the U.S. Lifesaving Service, sheltered shipwrecked sailors, and that mail through the area ran by the Barefoot Mailman, with a first post office named Zion.

Henry Flagler's Florida East Coast Railway reached the town in 1896 and gave farmers a way to ship crops. In 1905 local farmers formed a cooperative to run a canning plant for pineapples and tomatoes. In 1904 a Japanese agricultural colony called Yamato was established south of town, and its later resident George Morikami donated more than 200 acres, which is the land now holding the Morikami Museum and Japanese Gardens.

The Ladies Improvement Association, formed in 1902, pushed for a cemetery, a library, improvements on Atlantic Avenue and a town hall. The city's later civic history includes the S.D. Spady Cultural Heritage Museum, created in the former home of a teacher and principal, and a Historical Society formed in 1964.

Neighborhood ages differ widely across Delray Beach. Have the title company search for old easements and unreleased liens on an older parcel, because a long chain of ownership can hide an unsatisfied mortgage.

Can I keep my homestead benefit if I move within Florida?

Portability allows it. If you set up a new Florida homestead within three years of January 1 of the year you gave up the old one, the Save Our Homes difference can reduce the new home's assessed value. File Form DR-501T with Form DR-501 by March 1.

Homestead is lost if the property is rented, stops being your permanent home, or you stop being a Florida resident. Owners 65 or older may be offered an added exemption by local ordinance if household income is within the limit, so ask the Palm Beach County Property Appraiser whether one applies in Delray Beach.

More questions about Delray Beach, FL

When did Delray Beach become a city?

The City of Delray Beach was formed on May 11, 1927, when the Town of Delray Beach and the City of Delray united. The two had been incorporated separately, in 1923 and 1911.

What was Delray Beach called before?

It was first Linton, named in 1895 for a congressman in the settlement group. Residents changed it to Delray in 1898 after freezes damaged crops.

When are Palm Beach County property taxes delinquent?

April 1. Bills are payable from November 1 through March 31, and delinquent taxes cannot be paid online.

Is there an early payment discount in Palm Beach County?

Yes: 4 percent in November, 3 percent in December, 2 percent in January and 1 percent in February, with none in March.

The contract decides who pays, but all parties are liable. The statewide deed rate is 70 cents per $100 of consideration.

What are Weston sellers' quick-sale choices?

Weston sellers can go through an agent, a cash buyer or an investor, and the choice mostly comes down to how much time and certainty you need. Because most Weston homes sit inside a homeowners' association, the buyer's timeline often depends on association paperwork as well as financing.

Every buyer should write the price, closing date and who covers each closing charge into the contract. Then request the association's payoff or estoppel figures early, since an unpaid assessment can hold up the settlement.

How was Weston built out as a planned community?

Weston grew from a planned development rather than an old town. The city's history page says the area's 15,000 acres were assembled in the 1950s, that a Development of Regional Impact approved in 1978 first allowed more than 25,000 dwelling units, and that later amendments cut the figure to 17,000.

The Indian Trace Community Development District followed in 1981 to finance and manage water and sewer mains, water bodies and arterial roads. The development was renamed Weston, and by the page's account the first homes were finished in Windmill Ranch and Country Isles in 1984. By November 1991 the community had more than 5,000 residents.

Because the first homes date from 1984, Weston houses are comparatively recent. For a seller, the planned design means association rules and the district's roads, lakes and utilities are part of what the buyer is evaluating.

Why did Weston incorporate, and how does that touch a sale?

Weston's residents voted to form their own city rather than join a neighbor. The history page says a district board began an incorporation feasibility study in April 1994, appointed a nine member steering committee in May 1995, and asked Davie, Fort Lauderdale, Pembroke Pines and Sunrise for proposals on annexation.

By November 1995 the committee and the board concluded that a new city would serve residents best, since tax dollars generated in Weston would stay under local control and planning and zoning questions would be decided by residents. The board voted unanimously to file a local bill with the Broward Legislative Delegation, and the Legislature approved it on May 5, 1996.

For a seller, the result is a city that controls its own zoning and permits instead of the county. Ask the city, not the county, about setbacks, additions and pools, and give buyers the same instruction in writing.

Does a homeowners' association affect selling in Weston?

Very likely. The city's HOA page says most residences in Weston are in a private development governed by a homeowners' association, and that City Code requires each association to register annually with the City Clerk's Office by the first workday in April.

The same page explains that in gated or private communities the common areas are private property, so the association maintains the infrastructure, roads and landscaping inside. Trees on association property or street trees cannot be removed without a city permit, and the city maintains most of the water bodies, though some lakes are privately owned.

Homeowners who draw irrigation water from a lake or canal need the consent agreement the city publishes, and the city lists 954-385-2000 for questions. A buyer wanting to keep that irrigation should ask you for the agreement.

What building permit rules should a Weston seller check?

Start with the city's own rule on trees, because it is the one the HOA page states plainly: street trees and trees on association property cannot be removed without a city permit. Call Weston's Building Code Services and Planning and Zoning staff for any other exterior work, and ask what applies to the specific job.

Florida enacted a 2026 exemption for some small projects under $7,500, but it has limits. Electrical, plumbing and structural work still need permits in cities that have published their rules, so assume a permit is needed until Weston staff tells you otherwise.

If you finished a patio, pool deck or addition without a permit, ask the Building Department what it would take to close it out before a buyer's inspector finds it. Cash buyers may accept the risk, but expect them to reduce the offer for it.

How does the Broward County property tax cycle affect a Weston sale?

Unpaid taxes become delinquent April 1, and tax certificates on unpaid items are sold by June 1. Ask the Broward County tax office for the current bill and any delinquent balance when you request a payoff figure.

For homesteaded owners, Save Our Homes limits yearly assessment growth to the lower of 3 percent or the CPI change. The cap ends when the property changes hands, which resets the property to just value the next January 1. A Weston buyer can therefore face a higher bill than the seller paid.

An owner-occupant buyer can claim up to $50,000 of homestead exemption through Form DR-501, filed with the county appraiser by March 1, provided the home is their permanent residence by January 1. The exemption is lost if the home is rented or stops being the owner's permanent home.

If you will buy another Florida home, portability can move some of the accumulated savings to the new homestead when it is established within three years, using the forms the state revenue department lists.

What will the deed and recording cost in Weston?

Clerk recording charges under the statute are $5.00 on the first page and $4.00 on each page following, with trust fund and technology charges on top. Your title agent's settlement statement shows the final amounts. Check the figures against the contract before closing.

When did Weston become a city?

The State Legislature approved the local bill enabling the incorporation vote on May 5, 1996. The city's history page traces the road to incorporation from the 1978 Indian Trace approval.

Trees on association property and street trees cannot be removed without a city permit, per the city's HOA page. Call the city before any tree work.
